articles.title: Bring a tent, I've got the coffee: Lessons from it-sa
articles.raw_content:
Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

I'm just back from an interesting and demanding week of booth duty at it-sa Expo&Congress in Nuremberg, where Talos had a Point of Demonstration at the Cisco booth.

I personally see it-sa as the German or European counterpart to the RSA Conference in San Francisco, with a slightly different center of gravity in at least two dimensions.

First, the expo is the main event, not the congress. The congress is organized by associations, industry groups, and exhibitors, and plays more of a supporting role. Second, the focus is more local and European. Major topics were (of course) AI for defense tooling, securing AI systems themselves, and post-quantum cryptography. And here comes the local touch (in my opinion): digital sovereignty and regulatory compliance, with NIS2, CRA, and DORA.

But local doesn't translate to small, or to the city of Nuremberg. With more than 1,000 exhibitors and 33,000 visitors from 70 countries over three days of exhibition, preceded by a congress day, it was huge. Even as a trade show veteran, I was overwhelmed.

My conversations at the booth had a different focus, though. It was a lot of chatter about vulnerabilities like php2shell or broccoli2shell and state-sponsored actors, but again with a local touch: education.

I was very surprised how many teenagers stopped by to ask for advice. Here in Germany, you mainly have two paths for your career. One is the university route, and the other is vocational (apprenticeship). Across all industries the split is roughly 50 / 50 , while in IT it is more like 80% university, 20% apprenticeship. The common minimum age to start university is 18, while it is 16 for apprenticeships. Reality is way more complex, but the details don’t matter for the point I want to make.

For university opportunities in cyber, I count close to 30 bachelor programs . For apprenticeships, I count ZERO. There is the "IT Specialist" (Fachinformatiker), but it only has specializations like application development, system integration, digital networking, or data and process analysis. That is why an initiative exists to get an "IT Security" specialization going.

Even the degree route is thin. There are no official statistics, but my guess is 800 to 900 graduates a year, compared to a demand of more than 100,000. We need a second route into the field for the 16-year-old who finished various CTFs or Hack the Box challenges and wants to join the good side now. Honestly speaking, I would rather have them on our side of the fence at 16 than wonder at 26 where they ended up.

How does it look in your country?

On a personal note: If you consider visiting it-sa in 2027, book your accommodation early. The hotels are gone fast. That is the one downside, because Nuremberg isn't exactly a city with the infrastructure for more than 30,000 visitors. (Don't ask me how I learned that there are also camping spots close to the exhibition area.)

See you in Nuremberg next year. Bring a tent, just in case. I've got the coffee.

Cisco Talos recently discovered VOLTA , a mature, self-deleting Windows infostealer that uses AI to act as a personal intelligence analyst for cybercriminals. After harvesting a massive haul of credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to a large language model to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. The malware even uses stolen session access to enrich this data, searching the victim's emails for purchase receipts to corroborate home addresses. If an AI model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA seamlessly fails over to a multi-model chain to ensure the attackers get their prioritized dossier.

VOLTA replaces the manual work of data sorting with automated, AI-driven victim profiling. By letting an LLM determine a target's worth, attackers drastically reduce the human effort required to monetize stolen data. This commoditized threat allows even low-level actors to bypass security measures like Chrome's App-Bound Encryption and receive ranked target assessments, escalating the risk of severe follow-on attacks.

Organizations should implement application control policies to restrict or alert on processes launching Chrome with the --headless flag. Defenders must also enforce best practices for storing credentials in hardware-backed stores.

Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. For more information and sample details, read the full blog .

AI agents used by Railway breach systems of rival Primcloud This one is juicy. According to Primcloud’s founder, Railway’s agents used credentials from inside their own application’s containers to request every secret from Primcloud customers and employees and then twice port-scanned all 65,536 addresses on the company’s network. ( Security Boulevard ) ( X )

Europe on alert after supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks in 10 countries A significant increase in freezer temperature has forced retailers to discard food in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Germany, and Sweden. Beyond supermarkets, cold storage for French plasma stock were affected, as well. ( BBC ) ( The Register )

Binance reveals how fake job interviews and AI tool abuse led to $6.43B theft Binance said the record-setting theft was the culmination of a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" that involved the use of a tampered Homebrew installation and recruitment-themed social engineering attack targeting two of its engineers. ( The Hacker News )

AI threats create urgent need to renew cybersecurity information-sharing law, businesses tell Congress After the law’s initial 10-year operating period expired in 2025, lawmakers passed several short-term extensions, with the latest one set to lapse on Dec. 11. Cybersecurity experts and industry leaders have repeatedly urged lawmakers to renew the law. ( Cybersecurity Dive )

Cops bust botnet of 1.3M infected Android TV boxes Security firms working with Japan’s National Police Agency has disrupted XCPE, a backdoor used to build a massive botnet comprising more than 1.3 million Android devices across more than 200 countries. ( The Register )

The VOLTA infostealer: Outsourcing cybercrime grunt work to AI Ryan Fetterman breaks down the newly discovered infostealer. Unlike traditional stealers, VOLTA integrates LLMs to analyze stolen credentials in real-time, effectively turning raw data into a prioritized, high-value dossier for the attacker.

Stealing AI secrets and breaking EDRs Phishing may have dropped from last quarter's highs, but ransomware engagements climbed as attackers shifted their focus toward disabling EDR systems and scraping AI credentials. The financial sector also returned as a top target.

NIK C2: The new AI-enabled command-and-control framework NIK C2 contains a Windows implant, using which, an actor can dump credentials, stream the victim's keystrokes to collect the targeted victim’s sensitive data, and instruct an integrated AI model to analyze the harvested data, all within the compromised session.

articles.title: Appraisal by AI: Model-driven victim prioritization in the VOLTA infostealer
articles.raw_content:
VOLTA is a mature stealer implant with an optional AI-integration layer. After stealing credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets, VOLTA sends a structured evidence bundle to an LLM to rank the victim’s assets by monetization value. If a model refuses to perform the target assessment, VOLTA fails over to a three-model chain, implying a direct engineering effort and expectation of hitting model guardrails. This stealer is self-deleting, and there is no attacker-owned infrastructure. The novelty in the AI-integration is that it is not supporting a traditional malware capability but working as an intelligence analyst on behalf of the operator. There is a new idea in the cybercrime world — cast a wide net, steal everything, and let AI sort out the specifics. A new malware self-named “VOLTA-AUTODOXER,” surfaced through the CAIRN research effort , is a self-deleting Windows infostealer that augments its post-theft workflow with an LLM-powered victim-profiling stage. After harvesting the standard stealer haul, including browser passwords; cookies; payment cards; cryptocurrency wallet seed phrases; Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox sessions; Microsoft OAuth tokens; SSH and cloud-provider keys; Wi-Fi profiles; and screenshots, VOLTA builds a structured evidence bundle about the person behind the machine. This bundle contains geolocation and home address, employer and employer domain, inferred birth year, card last-4 digits, Slack workspaces, document authorship metadata, iPhone backup indicators, and a live Roblox account valuation. It then uses stolen session access to enrich that bundle further: searching the victim's Gmail for purchase receipts to corroborate a home address, pulling UberEats and DoorDash order history, and enriching Discord accounts via the stolen token. The bundle is serialized and POSTed to OpenRouter under a system prompt that instructs the model to act as "a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment." The required output includes a section titled “WHAT THEY'RE WORTH” with valuables ranked by monetization with a low/medium/high tier, and a section on “THEIR OPSEC” containing an assessment of the victim's security posture and password hygiene. The model is the operator's triage analyst; it turns a raw credential log into a prioritized and citation-backed dossier of the victim and their monetizable assets. Figure 1. The VOLTA-AUTODOXER workflow. The AI configuration: “Go deep, not wide... Be blunt, specific, accurate.” VOLTA uses a multi-model architecture to fall back resiliently if it hits a model’s refusal, checking each response for phrases like “I can’t” or “I’m not able,” before passing on to a chain of up to three models. Endpoint https[ :]// openrouter [ .]ai/ api /v1/chat/completions Default model anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 Fallback chain moonshotai /kimi-k2 → google/gemini-2.5-flash Temperature 0.2 — deterministic, consistent output Request format Hand-assembled JSON; no SDK; User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 Figure 2. Hardcoded model selection. Figure 3. Failover model selection to kimi-k2, and then gemini-2.5-flash. Model temperate controls the randomness and predictability of LLM-generated text. The low hardcoded temperature value (0.2) suggests the attacker is emphasizing accuracy and consistency. The malware also employs a chain of cascading models in the event of failures. This multi-model architecture suggests that the operator is anticipating encountering refusals, with the fallback pivoting to a few, smaller, and more permissive models. The system prompt directly reveals the operator’s use case: Produce a concise analytical assessment of the victim’s suitability as a target, backed by an auditable trail of citations. Figure 4. VOLTA's raw system prompt. The prompt also asks for something out of the ordinary, but that agents excel at: making connections between sparse and disparate data. For example, encouraging connections like the victim’s names, addresses, or universities to patterns in their passwords. In this case, the model isn't being asked to find data; rather, it’s being asked to stretch the data and make useful inferences that extend the value of what has been scraped. Stealer capabilities VOLTA’s capabilities are directly aligned with the records produced in modern digital life, and well beyond basic credential theft. In a single pass, the stealer can extract browser credentials, cookies, and saved payment cards across Chromium-based browsers. It hits Firefox and Thunderbird, Outlook profiles, Slack workspaces, Steam and Battle.net sessions, Discord tokens, Telegram sessions, Roblox accounts, and SSH and cloud-provider config files (gcloud, OpenVPN, Hide.me). VOLTA doesn’t just copy cryptocurrency wallets, but runs an embedded cracker against the vault inline, writing the result to a WALLET VAULTS CRACKED line in its own report. Every saved Wi-Fi password on the machine is pulled via a direct call to WlanGetProfileList and dumped to plaintext. Figure 5. VOLTA dumps plaintext passwords for every saved Wi-Fi network on the host. Figure 6. The organized collection targets. What really sets VOLTA apart from commodity stealers is what comes after the initial collection. There is a live enrichment pass that leverages stolen sessions to deep dive the victim’s data. For example, using the victim's own authenticated Gmail tokens, it queries their inbox for receipts from Amazon, DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub, Walmart, and PayPal, then review those receipts to establish a confirmed home address. Stolen Uber Eats and DoorDash sessions are called directly for order history. The Discord token is re-used to enrich the victim's account profile. Roblox inventory is valued via a live “Rolimons[.]com” lookup. Figure 7. That’s right: Your Uber Eats history is now a potential liability. After the collection and enrichment stages are complete, the data is assembled and structured locally in a file called “Identity_Report.txt”. This file is serialized into a bundle as JSON and POSTed to OpenRouter along with the system prompt. The returned payload is received as “AI_Analysis.txt”. Both files exfil together in “volta_dox.zip”. Figure 8. VOLTA’s exfil can happen in three stages: 1) after the stealer runs (“volta_log.zip”), 2) after the AI call (“volta_dox.zip”), (3) if the network enrichment produces anything (“volta_doxnet.zip”). The inference round-trip happens entirely through the victim's own network connection, on their own machine, before the result is exfiltrated. Deployment model Instead of hardcoding its Telegram channel, API keys, and settings directly into the code (which is likely what someone writing a tool for personal use would do) VOLTA uses a template with six swappable slots, filled in at build time. This suggests it’s a builder model: The author sells access, the customer provides their values, and the builder compiles a custom binary for each order. The credentials in those slots are encrypted, but not in a meaningful way. The key is SHA-256 of two constants sitting in the same binary, but it's presumably there because customers expect their API keys not to be sitting in plaintext, not because it provides real protection. Anyone who reverses the file can recover them. If VOLTA is indeed a commoditized malware, then the AI dossier capability isn't something the author invented for their own operations. It is a feature which enables a customer of any level of sophistication to point it at victims and start receiving ranked target assessments in their Telegram inbox. All the observed endpoints for this malware are third-party controlled. There is no actor-owned infrastructure. Countermeasures Much of the token-stealing capability of VOLTA relies on techniques to bypass App-Bound Encryption (ABE) in Chrome. An application control policy that restricts which processes may launch Chrome with --headless would block the ABE decryption path entirely. At minimum, you can also alert when Chrome is launched with --headless from any process not in a known developer. Best practices for storing credentials in hardware backed stores also apply. In the event of compromise, the main executable may have deleted itself, but users should attempt to preserve the “APPDATA%\volta_debug.txt” file. This is a timestamped harvest log and contains a record of exactly what was collected and whether the LLM call succeeded. Revoke any potentially compromised tokens and change passwords. For cryptocurrency wallets, if the seed phrase was in plaintext on disk, treat the wallet as fully compromised and migrate funds to a new wallet with a seed generated on an air-gapped device. Conclusions VOLTA is a mature stealer with a late-stage AI layer added for one purpose: relieving the operator of analytical work. The axis of AI improvement here is not speed or scale but effort displacement; the same logic visible in CLOSEDQUORUM , though applied to a different phase. These implants reflect the same underlying logic: Identify the step that requires the most sustained human attention and replace it with a model call. The question for defenders is not whether this pattern will appear elsewhere, but which phase it touches next. Figure 9. End-to-end VOLTA workflow. The second trend to watch is the anticipation of hitting model refusals, and the approaches to building in resiliency. In this case, it includes a fallback chain from Claude to Kimi to Gemini and the ability to run without the LLM stage altogether if no key is present. As AI integration in malware matures, refusal resilience may become a standard design requirement. The open question underlying both trends is whether effort displacement in crimeware changes the landscape in a meaningful way: lowering the operational floor, raising the ceiling on scale, or both. Cybercrime operations have always been opportunistic, and the sophistication bar has always been lower than assumed, but there is a difference between a wide net and a wide net that sorts itself. Sample details SHA256 57ef4242666d78c50df145b34023df564f0fad38812d6a580e66433d427e2279 Filename 9BY0tjwOc3ut.exe / yLP9m5J3i2Aw.exe Type PE32+ x86-64 PE Timestamp 2026-08-17 20:35 First Seen (UTC) 2026-10-11 12:46

The self-deleting VOLTA infostealer steals credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets. Then, it uses LLMs to profile victims and rank their most valuable assets.

articles.title: A quiet week in infosec <.<
articles.raw_content:
Welcome to this week’s edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

“The darkest period of my life, so far, arrived the summer I was pregnant with my eldest son. The future was growing in me with all of its terrifying unpredictability, and I found myself anxious, unable to work and woefully at sea.” — Lauren Groff

I doubt Lauren had this maniacal infosec news cycle in mind when she wrote about the terrifyingly unpredictable future, but honestly, she’s got our current careers down cold. Let he who is not woefully at sea cast the first water balloon? I’ll work on it. Here we are with PHP taking up every available ounce of oxygen, Node.js adding its own spice to the sauce... and here’s me, staring my screen blankly, waiting for an original thought to leak out and onto this page. Not to worry, none have. There is simply nothing novel to say because the entire internet has it covered. In triplicate. With graphs and compelling statistics and AI-generated evil bad guy images galore.

These vulnerabilities are serious, and the remediations matter. Teams need to know what they run, find the affected systems, and get them patched and determine ways to secure systems that can’t be patched. I’m simply not going to add another dramatic headline to the stack or pretend there’s a clever new angle hiding in the margins. The thing I keep looping on is that the work underneath the headlines is familiar and it’s the real story. To defend your environment, you need a team that knows that environment, has enough time and expertise to investigate the telemetry, that can tell an anomaly from the usual benign noise, and take action. Yes, the right tools help, and without them you can’t do it — but the people doing the work are still what make those tools useful.

Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. This is the entire ballgame. Read it again: Give smart people enough room to do smart people stuff. Because a good response starts way before the headline. Know what you own, who owns it, what version is running, whether it can be reached from the internet, what identities can do what task on the device, etc. When a fix is available, make sure it actually reaches the system you meant to fix. If a system cannot be updated yet, give that exception an owner and a deadline. Reduce its exposure, add monitoring, and keep checking until the fix is in place. “We’ll get to it” is not a plan.

So, there may be nothing new to say about PHP this week, but the work is still worth talking about: Know your environment, take care of your team members, and keep paying attention when the weird thing stops being weird and starts becoming evidence. When the next headline arrives, help your teammate do the same.

“The only thing that makes life possible is permanent, intolerable uncertainty: not knowing what comes next.” — Ursula K. Le Guin

Cisco Talos has recently discovered "NIK C2," a new command-and-control framework that integrates AI directly into its attack chain. This Go-based Windows implant allows adversaries to dump credentials, stream keystrokes, and deploy screen-locking ransomware. It also uses an integrated OpenAI model to analyze harvested data on the fly. By hijacking the victim's own API keys to fund these requests, NIK C2 collapses data collection and exploitation into a single, continuous session.

By embedding a live AI pipeline directly into the C2 loop, NIK C2 turns a compromised host into an active operational asset rather than a passive foothold. Because it processes data and generates context-aware payloads locally, it erases the offline processing delays that historically gave defenders a critical detection window. Furthermore, by piggybacking on the victim's OpenAI account, threat actors completely mask their infrastructure, leaving no attributable trace and complicating incident response.

Defenders must embrace continuous behavioral vigilance. Ensure endpoint solutions monitor for unusual local proxy routing, unexpected PowerShell executions, and unauthorized access to browser databases or crypto wallets. Update your defenses using the ClamAV signature and indicators of compromise (IOCs) provided in the full blog .

CISA gives agencies days to patch critical PHP bugs CISA added the two vulnerabilities in the PHP open-source scripting software to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog Monday. ( Federal News Network )

Node2Shell: Brotli flaw triggers patching across Microsoft, Node.js, Python packages An out-of-bounds write in Google’s Brotli decoder affects Node.js, .NET, PowerShell, and Python packages, and can lead to code execution. ( SecurityWeek )

Gheist uses stolen GitHub tokens to steal private repository secrets via Actions logs Each workflow sits on a new branch named ci-sync- followed by six random characters. Deleting a branch, or the run it started, does not undo the exposure. ( The Hacker News )

Japan internet giant GMO says hackers posted stolen customer data GMO Internet is investigating a data leak after suspected unauthorized access to its Onamae cloud desktop service, which provides virtualized desktops to financial traders. ( TechCrunch )

Third Serengeti sweep tops 1,400 arrests as investigations mature Interpol's annual Operation Serengeti, now on its third iteration, led to 1,462 arrests across 20 African countries and the U.S., recovering $105 million in stolen funds. ( Dark Reading )

Stealing AI secrets and breaking EDRs Phishing may have dropped from last quarter's highs, but ransomware engagements climbed as attackers shifted their focus toward disabling EDR systems and scraping AI credentials. The financial sector also returned as a top target.

From federal SOCs to Talos: Ryan Fetterman on practical security research What does it mean to be "blue collar" for the blue team? Amy sat down with security researcher Ryan Fetterman to discuss his journey from federal agency work to his new role at Talos.

The Guy Who Invented Pain (plus first reactions to PHP2Shell) David Bianco built the Pyramid of Pain, so we offered him some more. David joins the Beers with Talos crew for a conversation how AI changes about his famous model, how EvidenceForge creates simulated incidents for research and training, and why his red-team entrance exam didn’t go to plan.

Compromised eMudhra intermediate certificates Cisco Talos is aware of eight compromised intermediate certificates belonging to the intermediate certificate authority. eMudhra has revoked the certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root.

Two critical RCEs in PHP core Two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP core could have implications across its wider ecosystem. This blog explains what we know so far, and details the Snort coverage available.

articles.title: IR trends Q3 2026: Actors impersonate IT help desks in vishing attacks as ransomware activity increases
articles.raw_content:
Phishing remained the leading initial access technique, appearing in slightly over one-third of all Cisco Talos Incident Response (Talos IR) engagements — a decrease from over 50 percent last quarter. In addition to traditional phishing links and attachments, we observed numerous threat actors conducting voice phishing (vishing) in tandem with IT desk impersonation to socially engineer the victim into allowing remote access via a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the next most common vector, accounting for one-third of Talos IR engagements. Threat actors predominantly targeted edge devices such as security gateways and remote network management interfaces. These are critical components within enterprise environments, often responsible for managing authentication, network traffic, or sensitive data. Compromising them can provide broad access to internal networks or user credentials. Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents made up 27 percent of engagements in Q3 2026, an increase from a maximum of 20 percent seen in the previous four quarters. Talos responded to attacks involving prolific, technologically advanced, and well-established ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) variants such as The Gentlemen, Qilin, and Rhysida, as well as Interlock, which operates as a closed group. Threat actors predominantly chose to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) systems, often by exploiting vulnerable drivers or using Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC). Additionally, we observed the emerging ransomware variant VYPR, whose operator(s) tested a range of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) instead of following a standard attack method or affiliate playbook. Talos experts discuss some of the biggest trends from the quarter in this video Sophisticated threat actors exploit public-facing application vulnerabilities for cyber espionage Talos IR continues to see prolonged cyber espionage intrusions targeting the telecommunications sector. Talos attributed most of these intrusions with high confidence to sophisticated threat actors involved in targeted attacks. The attackers in these intrusions routinely gain initial access by leveraging valid credentials and exploiting a known vulnerability (CVE-2023-20198) in publicly accessible web-based management interfaces—two of the most frequently observed initial access vectors this quarter. In one campaign, the threat actor deployed BadCandy, a malicious web shell implant known to be leveraged by Salt Typhoon, to maintain persistent and stealthy remote access. The adversaries continue to employ living-off-the-land (LOTL) tactics, leveraging legitimate network infrastructure features — such as VPN access, traffic mirroring, and management protocols — to establish backdoors, exfiltrate data, and conduct reconnaissance. Exploiting a vulnerability in the web-based management interface, they created privileged accounts, disabled logging to conceal their activity, and altered configurations to maintain persistence, blending their actions with normal administrative operations to evade detection. These intrusions revealed several security weaknesses in the victim environment, including reliance on password-only authentication without evidence of multi-factor authentication (MFA), use of legacy and weak management protocols (such as plaintext SNMP and outdated VPN encryption), and inadequate credential management practices. Attackers were able to create and abuse privileged accounts, disable logging, and manipulate configuration settings without encountering effective security barriers, enabling persistent and stealthy access. The absence of strong MFA and robust credential management are two of the most frequently observed security weaknesses this quarter. AI exploited as a weapon and a target Recent Talos IR investigations highlight the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in cybercriminal activity, both as a tool and a target. In one case, an internal threat actor who was hired under false credentials abused their privileged access to install AI-powered development tools, such as GitHub Copilot CLI and Anthropic Claude Code. While the investigation did not find evidence of malicious activity or data theft, the employee’s developer-level access — including cloning repositories, configuring plugins, and connecting to databases — could have enabled them to use AI tools to automate malicious actions within the organization. A second investigation revealed an attack chain in which a compromised macOS endpoint, infected via a trojanized application, was scripted to scrape credentials from the macOS keychain specifically associated with the Anthropic Claude Code AI assistant. This direct targeting of AI-related secrets highlights an emerging threat, where attackers seek to compromise not only traditional user and system credentials but also those tied to AI platforms, which may grant access to additional sensitive data and advanced automation capabilities. These incidents highlight the critical need for organizations to implement strong MFA and robust credential management practices, especially for AI platforms and development tools. Ransomware trends Ransomware and pre-ransomware incidents increased from a little over 20 percent last quarter to 27 percent in Q3, involving well-known threat groups like Interlock and the emerging ransomware VYPR. Frequently observed techniques involved deleting EDR systems and socially engineering victims into initiating remote management sessions. Emerging ransomware variant: VYPR During a Talos IR engagement, we observed a ransomware variant called “VYPR” that we assess is relatively new and still operationally immature. This assessment is supported by the absence of an established data leak site (DLS), as none was referenced in the ransom note and associated DLS infrastructure was not created until after the engagement. The group also appeared to rely on older leaked Conti-derived source code with only minimal modifications, reflecting a relatively unsophisticated technical approach. Their operations further suggested experimentation rather than a refined playbook, as they took an unusually long time to exfiltrate and encrypt data while testing different exfiltration parameters and deploying multiple vulnerable drivers to disable EDR protections. The actor gained initial access through voice phishing (vishing); they tricked a user into initiating a Microsoft Quick Assist session, allowing remote access to the endpoint. While the exact social engineering technique was not confirmed in this case, threat actors frequently impersonate IT help desks during vishing calls to manipulate victims into establishing remote connections — a tactic observed in several other Q3 engagements. The actor was then able to utilize existing RMM software, which subsequently executed PowerShell commands to download and install a Microsoft Software Installer (MSI) package from a remote IP address. During the attack, the actor leveraged tools that are commonly observed during ransomware investigations, including MeshAgent, Rclone, PsExec, IP scan, and Microsoft Terminal Services Client (MSTSC). Notably, we saw exfiltration over multiple days, which is not commonly observed during ransomware investigations. EDR killers: Why evade detection when you can destroy it? We observed several instances where ransomware operators disabled EDR systems, prioritizing direct disruption of security controls. We observed Interlock ransomware actors making multiple attempts to impair endpoint detection EDR capabilities by trying to uninstall Cisco Secure Endpoint (CSE) on compromised systems and used tools such as PsExec.exe and taskkill.exe to terminate security services and integrity checkers, including cscm.exe and sfc.exe. Additionally, the adversary disabled Windows Defender real-time protection and cleared various event logs to reduce visibility and hinder forensic analysis. This is in line with previously observed Interlock activity, where they deployed a malicious WDAC policy to terminate EDR solutions. In the previously mentioned VYPR ransomware incident, the threat actor disabled EDR and antivirus (AV) by using Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) techniques to evade detection and execute the ransomware. BYOVD attacks take advantage of trusted but flawed drivers to gain kernel-level access, enabling threat actors to disable EDR mechanisms and carry out their operations unimpeded. While this technique is commonly observed in ransomware attacks, this actor deployed an unusually large number of vulnerable drivers in the environment, possibly to create redundancies and maximize their chances of success. Targeting Targeting of the financial industry increased from last quarter to comprise 18 percent of all engagements, tying with public administration as the most targeted sector. Although the financial industry remains a valuable target, Talos has not ranked it among the top three most impacted sectors since 2024. One possible reason is that organizations in finance can typically invest more in cybersecurity, unlike sectors such as public administration, which has consistently been among the top-targeted industries over the past year. Meanwhile, health care fell to third place after ranking as the most targeted industry for the previous two consecutive quarters. Initial access While the number of engagements involving phishing as an initial access vector declined from last quarter, it remained the most common technique, appearing in 37 percent of Talos IR engagements. Exploitation of public-facing applications was the second most common initial access vector, accounting for 33 percent of engagements. Recommendations for addressing top security weaknesses The most common security weaknesses observed this quarter were insufficient logging, improper credential and secret management, and absent or improperly implemented authentication and MFA. These trends closely mirror last quarter, when insufficient logging and authentication weaknesses were also prevalent. Centralize logging and set retention requirements The leading security weakness was insufficient logging leading to visibility gaps, seen in over 40 percent of engagements this quarter. These gaps were in part due to the common threat actor practice of deleting logs, and in part due to insufficient log retention or configuration implemented by the customer. Talos IR recommends implementing a SIEM or centralized logging platform with a minimum of 90 days of retention, forwarding logs from servers, workstations, network infrastructure, cloud identity providers, and security appliances off-device so they survive log tampering and host rebuilds, and enabling process-creation, command-line, and cloud API (e.g., Microsoft Graph) auditing. Talos IR's Log Architecture Assessment service can identify gaps and provide a roadmap to a complete view of the environment. Tighten authentication and MFA controls Missing or insufficient authentication and MFA controls were the third most common security weakness this quarter, observed in 33 percent of engagements. The most prevalent issue was reliance on single-factor authentication, which allowed unauthorized access in several incidents. In many cases, legacy authentication protocols were still enabled, enabling adversaries to log in without any MFA requirements, and some environments failed to enforce MFA for high-privilege accounts. To reduce this risk, Talos IR recommends transitioning from push- and SMS-based MFA to phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and hardware security keys. Organizations should also restrict self-service MFA enrollment by requiring helpdesk verification, block legacy authentication through Conditional Access, enforce number matching or verified push where phishing-resistant methods are not yet feasible, and condition access on device compliance and trusted infrastructure rather than geographic location alone. Safeguard credentials and secrets Improper credential and secret management was the second most common security weakness seen in 33 percent of engagements this quarter, reinforcing the importance of security awareness training and consistent security hygiene for every user. Observed security issues included unsafe storage and handling of credentials, such as saving passwords in browser stores, poor control mechanisms like permitting autofill for browser-stored credentials, and credential reuse and sharing. Effective secret management begins with a formal process that covers passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates, and other sensitive credentials. By requiring unique passwords for every account and encouraging the use of password managers, organizations reduce the risks associated with credential reuse and sharing. Storing secrets securely, with encryption and access restricted to only those who need them, further strengthens protection. When credentials are no longer necessary or are suspected to be compromised, they should be promptly revoked and replaced. Regular reviews of access to privileged credentials, combined with thorough logging, help detect unusual activity. Equipping staff with training on safe handling and clear reporting procedures ensures that accidental disclosures are addressed quickly and effectively. Tales from the Frontlines: An exclusive briefing on Q3 incidents On November 12, Talos incident responders will be hosting an exclusive, unrecorded 30-minute webinar to review the most high-impact incidents our customers faced in Q3. Designed for security professionals of all levels, this is a candid discussion of what happened, how we handled it, and what it means for your organization. Registration is required to attend. Don't miss this chance to hear real-world stories from the frontlines of cyber defense, directly from the team who lived them. Register here MITRE ATT&CK appendix The table below represents MITRE ATT&CK techniques and tools observed in this quarter’s IR engagements, including relevant examples. Given that some techniques can fall under multiple tactics, we grouped them under the most relevant tactic based on the way they were leveraged. Please note that this is not an exhaustive list. Key findings from the MITRE ATT&CK framework include: The rise of phishing and the frequent use of valid accounts for initial access and lateral movement both highlight how attackers continue to rely on methods that have remained consistently effective year over year. Attacker success consistently reflects basic weaknesses in enterprise security posture, with persistent exploitation of known vulnerabilities — especially in internet-facing applications — demonstrating that adversaries continually scan for and opportunistically target unpatched systems. The most used techniques to maintain persistence were deploying web shells and creating scheduled tasks, demonstrating that attackers prioritize stealthy, reliable access by leveraging legitimate system components that blend in with normal operations. These techniques enable threat actors to maintain long-term control and quickly re-establish their presence even if some signs of compromise are removed. Tactic Technique Example Initial Access (TA0001) T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application Adversaries may exploit vulnerabilities in public-facing applications to gain unauthorized access to a network. T1566 Phishing (link, attachment, voice, service) Adversaries may rely on users clicking a malicious link or opening a malicious attachment to gain initial access, often using social engineering to increase success. T1078 Valid Accounts (Local, Domain, Cloud, SSH) Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts to access systems within the network and execute their payload. T1133 External Remote Services Adversaries may leverage remote services such as VPN or RDP to gain entry into an environment using legitimate access mechanisms. Execution (TA0002) T1059 Command and Scripting Interpreter (PowerShell, Windows/Unix Shell, JavaScript, Python) Adversaries may use built-in scripting interpreters like PowerShell or bash to execute malicious code on victim systems. T1610 Deploy Container Adversaries may deploy malicious containers in cloud or on-premises environments to establish execution. Per sistence (TA0003) T1505.003 Server Software Component: Web Shell Adversaries may install web shells on compromised servers to maintain per sistent access via HTTP/S. T1543 Create or Modify System Process (Windows Service, Scheduled Task) Adversaries may create or modify system processes, such as scheduled tasks or services, to maintain per sistence after initial compromise. T1136.001 Create Account: Local Account Adversaries may create new local accounts to establish per sistence or elevate privileges within the environment. T1562.001 Impair Defenses: Disable/ Modify Security Tools Adversaries may disable or modify security software and tools to avoid detection and facilitate continued o per ations. T1070 Indicator Removal (File Deletion, Clear Event Logs) Adversaries may remove or alter evidence of their activity by deleting files or clearing logs on compromised systems. T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information Adversaries may obfuscate files and information to prevent security tools from identifying malicious activity. T1218.011 System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32 Adversaries may use legitimate system binaries such as rundll32 to proxy execution of malicious code. T1222 File and Directory Per missions Modification Adversaries may modify file or directory per missions to conceal their presence or maintain access. T1055 Process Injection Adversaries may inject malicious code into the address space of legitimate processes to evade detection. T1550 Use Alternate Authentication Material Adversaries may use alternate authentication material, such as SSH keys, to access accounts without using passwords. Discovery (TA0007) T1018 Remote System Discovery Adversaries may enumerate remote systems on a network to identify targets for lateral movement or data collection. T1082 System Information Discovery Adversaries may collect detailed information about the o per ating system and hardware to inform later actions. T1087 Account Discovery (Domain Account) Adversaries may query for user and group information to identify accounts of interest in the environment. T1046 Network Service Discovery Adversaries may scan for open ports and network services to identify potential entry points or targets. T1518.001 Security Software Discovery Adversaries may search for installed security software to tailor evasion techniques accordingly. T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery Adversaries may gather network configuration details to better understand the environment and plan next steps. Command and Control (TA0011) T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer Adversaries may transfer tools or payloads into an environment to facilitate further o per ations. T1071 Application Layer Protocol (Web, DNS) Adversaries may use common web or DNS protocols for command and control to blend in with normal network traffic. T1219 Remote Access Software Adversaries may use legitimate remote access software to maintain control over compromised systems. T1572 Protocol Tunneling Adversaries may tunnel command and control traffic through allowed protocols to bypass network defenses. T1090 Proxy Adversaries may route communications through proxy servers to obscure their origin and evade detection. Lateral Movement (TA0008) T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares Adversaries may use SMB and admin shares to move laterally between systems within the network. T1021.004 SSH Adversaries may use SSH with stolen credentials or keys to move laterally across systems.
