articles.title: Parasitizing trust: How legitimate infrastructure becomes a delivery pipeline for attackers
articles.raw_content:
Legitimate infrastructure has become a powerful delivery mechanism for attackers, carrying the inherent trust they once had to build. As Cisco Talos explored in our previous research on weaponizing software-as-a-service (SaaS) notification pipelines , these platforms are increasingly repurposed as proxies for malicious intent.

Talos has since tracked a significant acceleration in this trend, observing abuse across more than 25 distinct legitimate platforms in the past year.

The abused infrastructure included collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment, and AI-related platforms.

This demonstrates that attackers are not limiting themselves to traditional phishing infrastructure or lookalike domains. Instead, they are systematically subverting the very tools businesses trust.

Talos recently analyzed two order notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines. Together, these campaigns accounted for roughly 1,400 messages observed by Talos.

The malicious element was not the outer sender identity, like a simple forged sender or lookalike domain. It was the content of the legitimate order notification workflow rendered. The suspicious content appeared inside the notification itself, in fields that would normally contain shipping information. The attacker’s objective was to use a trusted retail pipeline to create urgency around a high-value purchase and push the recipient toward an attacker-controlled phone number.

In the first campaign, the message appeared as a Staples order confirmation from "support@orders.staples.com” with the subject line, “Here’s your Staples order #9939818875. Thanks for shopping with us.” The body displayed a plausible purchase for an Apple iPad, including order number, delivery timing, pricing, billing information and standard Staples footer content. The suspicious element was embedded in the order details: “Helpline 806 283 7712,” “Order Confirmed,” and the Staples corporate address appeared in fields normally associated with shipping or billing information.

The structure of the message matters. The attacker was not trying to persuade the user to click a crude phishing link. Instead, the message created the impression that an expensive order had already been placed and that the fastest way to resolve it was to call the embedded “helpline.” The desired user action was a phone call. Once the victim moved from email to voice, the attacker could continue the scam through social engineering, payment manipulation, credential theft, or remote assistance fraud.

The headers reinforced the trust problem. The Staples message showed DKIM alignment for “orders.staples.com” and DMARC passed for the visible Staples domain. The message also passed through forwarding and re-encapsulation paths, including Proton Mail, Microsoft 365, and downstream enterprise mail infrastructure. These hops complicate provenance analysis, but they do not change the core issue: Authentication helped establish that the outer message was credible, while offering no assurance that the phone number or transaction context was legitimate.

The second campaign used the same pattern in a Dell order received notification. The message was sent from “Dell | Order Received <received@order.dellcom>” with the subject line, “We have your order | Dell Purchase ID: 2009829958247.” The body presented a purchase for Microsoft Project Standard 2024, totaling $736.09. As with the Staples example, the suspicious content appeared in transaction fields. The “Ship To” and “Bill To” sections included “Confirmed Order,” “Helpline 808 232 6397,” and “Call Our Sales Team”.

The Dell message used the same psychological lever: an unexpected high-value purchase, a legitimate-looking order template, and a phone number positioned as the path to resolution. The attacker did not need the recipient to trust a new domain or unfamiliar brand. The message borrowed credibility from Dell’s order pipeline and redirected the recipient toward attacker-controlled contact information.

Authentication results showed DKIM passing for Dell-related infrastructure and DMARC passing for “order.dell.com”. As with the Staples sample, forwarding artifacts and SRS-style return paths appeared as the message moved through Microsoft and enterprise mail infrastructure. But the malicious intent did not live in an obviously forged sender. It lived inside the rendered order content.

These campaigns illustrate the same trust-boundary failure described in our earlier research on platform-as-a-proxy (PaaP) abuse. In those cases, attackers placed malicious content into SaaS fields that trusted platforms later rendered into notifications. Here, the same concept appears in commerce infrastructure, in the retailer’s order pipeline. The attacker supplies the intent, while the trusted system performs the delivery.

From a defensive perspective, sender authentication is necessary, but it is not sufficient. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC help answer whether a message came from expected infrastructure. However, they do not answer whether the transaction was legitimate, whether the rendered fields make business sense, or whether the user is being pushed toward an attacker-controlled action.

Order notifications should be treated as sensitive content. Any field reflected into a transactional message — shipping name, billing name, address line, company name, order note, support field, or fulfillment instruction — can become a delivery vehicle if it is not validated before rendering. Retailers and security teams should correlate order notification content with account history, payment state, shipping context, and known support channels. Transactional templates should reject or flag unexpected phone numbers, URLs, urgency language, and support instructions when they appear in fields where they do not belong.

In both campaigns, the wrapper was legitimate enough to inherit trust. The payload was attacker-influenced. That distinction is the center of this attack class.

The abuse of commerce pipelines is merely one manifestation of a broader, systemic vulnerability. Whether the attacker initiates a fake purchase or a fraudulent account sign-up, the root cause remains the same: Platforms are implicitly trusting data that enters their systems from untrusted sources, only to render that data into high-reputation, automated notifications. This same mechanism of reflection — where input is echoed back into an email to a third party — is the engine behind an evolution in list bombing, moving the attack from simple denial-of-service to a sophisticated vehicle for content delivery.

List bombing is an abuse technique in which attackers submit a victim’s email address to numerous legitimate registration, subscription or notification workflows, flooding the inbox with automated messages. While this vector is traditionally viewed as a denial-of-service or distraction tactic designed to bury critical alerts in a flood of junk, Talos has observed a subset of cases where this behavior is being repurposed as a delivery vehicle for malicious content. This abuse occurs when an attacker identifies public-facing registration, profile, or project-naming forms that lack sufficient input validation. By inputting a "hostile string" — such as a cryptocurrency-themed lure — into fields intended for a name, company, or title, the attacker forces the platform to treat this data as legitimate user information. When the service reflexively incorporates this input into its automated welcome, verification, or notification templates, the system acts as an unintended carrier, delivering the attacker’s content inside a high-reputation, system-generated email that can pass standard authentication checks.

The attacker’s objective in these cases is to bypass the security perimeter by laundering their malicious content through the brand reputation of a trusted service provider. While this is not yet a broad industry shift, it represents a calculated abuse of a platform's trust boundary. By embedding their lure in an automated notification, the adversary ensures that the message arrives with the appearance of administrative legitimacy, significantly increasing the likelihood that the recipient will trust the content. The goal is to reach the target's inbox with enough platform authority that the message may be evaluated as routine notification traffic rather than attacker-controlled content.

Beyond the risk to the individual recipient, this vector creates a significant brand liability. When a service provider’s infrastructure is used to broadcast fraudulent content, the resulting user complaints and bounce-backs can degrade the platform's own sender reputation, potentially triggering blocklisting that impacts their legitimate business communications.

The final vector moves the abuse pattern into the mail system itself. Instead of relying on a retailer, SaaS platform, or registration workflow to generate the message, the attacker attempts to make a delivery status workflow carry attacker-controlled content.

Bounces, formally known as delivery status notifications (DSNs) or non-delivery reports (NDRs), are generated when a message cannot be delivered. Under normal conditions, a mail system sends the delivery report back to the original SMTP envelope sender. Depending on the implementation, that report may include the original headers, portions of the message body, URLs, attachments, or an encapsulated copy of the failed message. That returned content creates the abuse opportunity.

In one example Talos observed, a mail delivery system notification carried a WeTransfer-themed file-sharing lure. The administrative wrapper made the message look like routine mail-system noise, while the nested content asked the recipient to engage with what appeared to be a file transfer workflow. The attacker’s goal was to make the phishing lure feel less like an unsolicited external message and more like part of a technical delivery failure that required review. Users are conditioned to view system errors as benign and are far more likely to engage with an "administrative" fix than a suspicious, standalone phishing email.

There are several ways this kind of message can reach a victim. In opportunistic backscatter, an attacker sends mail using the victim’s address as the forged envelope sender. If an intermediate system accepts the message and later fails to deliver it, the resulting DSN may be sent back to the forged sender. If the DSN includes enough of the original message, the bounce itself can carry the lure.

A second possibility is intentional bounce abuse, where the attacker uses an authenticated, compromised, or otherwise controllable sending context to trigger a delivery failure that returns attacker-influenced content. This differs from an outright forged NDR, where the attacker simply fabricates the bounce message and sends it directly. From the recipient’s mailbox, however, these cases can look similar: A delivery-failure wrapper contains content the attacker wants the user to trust.

This distinction matters for defenders. A DSN’s administrative appearance does not validate the content inside it. The outer message may be a legitimate delivery report, while the returned or encapsulated content may still contain a phishing link, credential harvesting page, malicious attachment, or social engineering prompt.

Across these vectors, the defensive failure is consistent: Trusted infrastructure is being treated as a shortcut for trusted content.

Sender authentication remains essential. SPF, DKIM, DMARC, reputation, and infrastructure analysis help determine whether a message came from an expected source. But these controls do not answer a separate and increasingly important question: What was that trusted system instructed to carry?

Order notifications, registration workflows and delivery reports all create opportunities for attacker-influenced content to appear inside messages that users and security tools are conditioned to trust. In the Staples and Dell campaigns, the suspicious content was a phone number placed into transactional fields. In list bombing and registration abuse, the lure can appear inside reflected account or profile data. In bounce abuse, the malicious content may sit inside returned message data or a nested MIME object.

Defending against this requires content-aware validation at multiple points in the delivery chain. Platform owners should treat any user-controlled value rendered into an email template as untrusted data. Fields used for names, addresses, company names, project titles, order notes or support instructions should be validated before storage and again before rendering. Phone numbers, URLs, markup, line breaks, and urgent support language should be rejected or flagged when they appear in fields where they do not belong.

Security gateways should inspect the fully rendered message, not only the sender or template. That includes HTML, text, URLs, redirects, attachments, personalization fields, and nested MIME content. For transactional email, defenders should also evaluate whether the message content aligns with the workflow that produced it. An order notification containing unexpected support numbers, cancellation instructions, or high-urgency language should be treated differently from a routine receipt.

For delivery reports, recursive MIME inspection is especially important. Gateways should parse DSN containers, extract returned messages or message fragments, and apply normal phishing, malware, and URL analysis to the nested content. A bounce should explain a delivery failure, not provide a blind path for untrusted payloads.

The broader lesson is that attackers are no longer only exploiting technical vulnerabilities in infrastructure. They are exploiting the assumptions built into business processes. When legitimate systems render attacker-influenced data into trusted notifications, the result can pass authentication checks and still deliver malicious intent.

Defenders should therefore treat sender trust and content trust as separate but complementary signals. The wrapper can explain where a message came from. It cannot prove that the payload is safe.

Special thanks to Eric Peterson, Dev Shah, and Adam Katz for their professional guidance and input during the development of this research.

The self-deleting VOLTA infostealer steals credentials, sessions, and cryptocurrency wallets. Then, it uses LLMs to profile victims and rank their most valuable assets.

Talos and Recorded Future identified UAT-6275 activity targeting government organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States. Recovered artifacts show additional interest in water resources and energy.

Cisco Talos identified an APT spear-phishing campaign against individuals affiliated with Taiwan research organizations. The operation leveraged legitimate public event themes and impersonated reputable academic and policy institutions.

articles.title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
articles.raw_content:
Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model.

Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited.

We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines.

With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains.

The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from?

As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions:

If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed?

Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old?

Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed?

How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers?

Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end?

The answer to many of these questions boils down to this: The majority of these vulnerabilities are coming from repositories of old code from large-profile products and systems; and disclosure does not equal weaponization.

AI is chewing through a backlog of technical debt in libraries and tools used as the dependable, best-practice lynchpins of so many environments. These models have a new perspective, an ability to "think" without some of the hangups or assumptions of human defenders, and they are thorough in listing those vulnerabilities.

Entrenched older tools have always been prime targets because of their predictability; attackers know those tools and all their secrets, and they know what is likely to be present in a network with them. Multi-exploit attacks can be deployed with little variability.

Pre-Mythos threat actors exploited log4j ( CVE-2021-44228 ) to immense success. The library was ubiquitous, included in nearly every environment, but not a component that got cataloged in visibility scans. A combination of scale and low visibility meant defenders were blindsided, scrambling to find out if they even used the log4j library before starting to concoct a mitigation plan.

Talos has ongoing relationships with some of the largest technical vendors (such as the Microsoft Active Protections Process ( MAPP ) agreement). Organizations share additional information—detection guidance or maybe a POC — for vulnerabilities that are most likely to be exploited, to enable Talos to provide adequate coverage when the advisories are announced.  "Microsoft believes it is important for us to provide detection content, based on their guidance," as Yves Younan, Director of Talos Vulnerability Discovery, Detection, and Testing, says.

Talos has needed to invest more resources to get coverage in on time for critical vendors like Microsoft to keep up with notifications coming in fast and often on staggered or out-of-band timelines.

For larger vendors, the pressure is handleable for now. However, open-source projects are getting flooded. Some projects have a trusted group that can combine to tackle patches, and some share with the full community for immediate assistance, but it is up to the project. The internet runs on open-source work.

The pace of discovery presents a challenge for the traditional coordinated disclosure system vulnerability hunters have been using for years, and some are calling it into question.

Security vulnerabilities should be reported, to enable an informed defender base and regular patching, and vendors responsible for vulnerable code need time to create coverage. A timed disclosure model where notifications are sent to a vendor, who then has a set period of time (typically 90 days) to provide coverage before the disclosure is released publicly, has created a more secure online environment for decades.

Now, many practitioners are releasing advisories publicly without a disclosure period beforehand. The reasoning is that if one AI can find a weakness, any other could, so the vulnerability is already, effectively, released.

This conversation is actively changing expectations around vulnerability disclosure, and guidance is in flux.

No one knows the future, but we can always look to the past for insight.

Numbers of vulnerabilities jump drastically when a new bug class is identified, as their possibilities are explored to the fullest. Then the discoveries plateau and drop off.

When format string vulnerabilities were discovered as a new bug class in 2000, the initial influx of discoveries ramped up and up, until reaching a peak in 2005 and then slowly declining over the next couple of years. Format string vulnerabilities are still discovered, but they are a smaller overall fraction of the number of CVEs discovered in a year.

Theoretically, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery could go the same way.

While frontier models have not discovered a new vulnerability class, they are more efficient at discovering known types of software vulnerabilities. Given that a lot of vital software has a long history of code releases, there’s plenty of code to mine for weaknesses. But there’s only so much code… right?

Old and commonly used tools are often under the highest scrutiny, lending them one kind of safety: Because of their popularity, utility, and stability, when popular tools have vulnerabilities, they are discovered fast and patched promptly.

As the historical backlog of essential systems is turned over by AI, vulnerabilities will be found and patched. New code will ideally be run through AI bug-checkers that will prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced. The rate of new vulns should level off and drop accordingly.

There are some caveats. In the past, as vulnerability disclosures increased through coordinated disclosures, we saw increased adoption of mitigations. Exploitation became significantly harder. Attackers often need to chain together 3 or more vulnerabilities to successfully exploit a system.

However, more awareness of vulnerabilities often leads to more exploitation. Attackers often use vendor patches meant to protect customers to discover where vulnerabilities might exist. The frequency of patching has delayed human attackers via parsing bottlenecks, but AI can eliminate that problem.

The volume is certainly up.

Fresh as this blog is being finished, the October Patch Tuesday dropped almost 500 more than last month.

With refinement, any vulnerability could become a link to a path of effect. But... not all vulnerabilities are exploitable. Some are wildly impractical for attacker use. In fact, the percent of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) is vastly smaller than the found vulnerabilities.

Of the 975 vulnerabilities Microsoft reported in September, there were only three in-the-wild exploits detected. When viewed by percentage, vulnerabilities versus KEVs tell a different and perhaps reassuring story.

Compared with the same period last year, additions to the known-exploited vulnerability list increased by 37%, while published CVEs increased by 105%. However, we wouldn't necessarily expect those figures to grow in proportion. Adversaries only need enough useful vulnerabilities to compromise their targets, and the same vulnerabilities can be reused against many organizations. The KEV count tracks distinct vulnerabilities known to be exploited, not the number of attacks or successful compromises.

AI helps ingest code, advisory reports, and attack surfaces with inhuman speed, but it cannot currently make judgment calls about the value of a weakness.

For defenders, the question remains the same: Which vulnerabilities provide a viable path into their environment, and how do you close those paths?

The undeniable danger here is in exploitation time going down rapidly, while the vulnerabilities that could become exploits is still going up. The biggest hurdle for a defender is determining what is a real vulnerability for their environment, and what is not.

Different defenders have different forms of control depending on their role.

For those who are writing code, the new standard validation chain should include AI evaluation by models at least as up to date as those being used to hunt for vulnerabilities. It is relatively cheap to run new code through AI, but very expensive to run a cumbersome backlog of old code through. Bite it off in chunks.

For those whose role involves keeping the tools ready: Upgrade ASAP.  Don't stop there.

For Cisco customers, implement LiveProtect to mitigate vulnerabilities between advisory release day and patching, to give time for that patching. Do this for everything you own.

Move beyond static domain blocking and implement behavioral detection that alerts on anomalous traffic patterns directed toward automation platforms.

Hone your focus to the vulnerabilities with the highest exploitability in your environment. KEVs are far less common among the sea of advisories, and their numbers have not risen proportionally with the AI-assisted deluge.

Focus on building defense-in-depth. Employ multiple protection systems, to cover for delays in patching. Implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), create custom IPS/Snort triggers to block pre-patched traffic using SnortML, deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models in software build chains.

Dive deeper into this conversation with the latest TTP interview with Yves Younan and vulnerability researcher Bella Fusari.

For more numbers and advice for defenders:

Don't swing at everything

Threat Source Newsletter: Discovery ≠ Exploitation

The cybersecurity community has seen examples of autonomous agents, built inside AI labs, attacking public infrastructure. How you prepare for agentic threats is what makes the difference during real incidents.

What really frustrates an adversary? Eight Cisco Talos researchers share practical ways to make their next move slower and riskier, from deception and behavioral detection to breaking attack dependencies and resisting manufactured urgency.

Advances in AI technology will continue to identify vulnerabilities that in some circumstances are difficult, or effectively impossible, to patch. Appropriate network segmentation, rigorous visibility, and the deployment of NGFW/IPS combinations can provide a powerful compensatory layer.

articles.raw_content:
IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics The statistics in this report are based on detection verdicts returned by Kaspersky products unless otherwise stated. The information was provided by Kaspersky users who consented to sharing statistical data. Quarterly figures In Q3 2026: Kaspersky products blocked more than 311 million attacks launched from online resources. Web Anti-Virus responded to 47 million unique links. File Anti-Virus blocked more than 23 million malicious and potentially unwanted objects. There were 4470 new ransomware variants discovered. More than 81,000 users experienced ransomware attacks. 15% of all ransomware victims whose data was published on threat actors’ data leak sites (DLSs) were victims of Qilin. More than 217,000 users were targeted by miners. Ransomware Quarterly trends and highlights Threat actor disruption In August, the creator and lead administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation was sentenced to 16 years in prison. The convict developed the ransomware Trojan and at the time of his arrest played a central role in the RaaS operation: running the affiliate program, recruiting affiliates, supplying them with information and attack tools, working with initial access brokers, communicating with victims, and processing payments. In September, a member of the Ryuk RaaS group was sentenced to two years in prison and three years of supervised release. In 2019 and 2020, he and his accomplices breached organizations’ networks and encrypted data with the Ryuk Trojan. According to public reports, hundreds of workstations and servers were compromised. According to the prosecution, the attacker received a total of about 1610 BTC in ransom payments from victims. Also in September, a member of the Conti RaaS group was sentenced to four years in prison. He was charged with attacking companies in 2021 and 2022. In addition to carrying out attacks, he developed part of the group’s malware toolkit. Vulnerabilities and attacks In July, researchers published a report on the Qilin group exploiting the CVE-2026-0257 vulnerability in Palo Alto Networks firewall software. The vulnerability allowed attackers to bypass authentication and compromise victims’ networks without valid accounts. CISA published information in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog (KEV) on several CVEs actively exploited by ransomware groups: CVE-2026-15409 / CVE-2026-15410 in SonicWall SMA1000 remote access gateways. CISA doesn’t specify which groups exploited these vulnerabilities, but researchers have linked this activity to INC Ransom. CVE-2026-45659 in Microsoft SharePoint Server allowed an authenticated, low-privileged attacker to achieve remote code execution. CVE-2025-60710 in Microsoft Windows allowed attackers to escalate privileges locally. CVE-2026-59310 in VMware vCenter enabled unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2025-14733 in WatchGuard Firebox also enabled unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-63077 in JetBrains TeamCity allowed OS commands to run with the privileges of the TeamCity server process by way of an authentication bypass through the agent polling protocol. Command execution at that level could give access to configurations, credentials, CI/CD pipelines, and more. The most prolific groups This section highlights the most prolific ransomware gangs by number of victims added to each group’s DLS. Qilin (15.39%) holds first place, as it did last quarter. Qilin is followed by The Gentlemen (7.89%), which was especially active in Q1 but did not make the list in Q2. A notable newcomer on the list is Deadlock (4.46%), a relatively young ransomware family first reported in July 2025. Miners Number of new miner variants In Q3 2026, Kaspersky solutions detected 2197 new miner variants. After the spike in the second quarter, it’s fair to say the pattern has returned to the calmer one typical of last year. Attacks on macOS Quarterly highlights At the beginning of the third quarter, Jamf researchers discovered a new stealer, PamStealer. What sets it apart is its use of Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) to verify the administrator password the user enters. During the quarter, Socket researchers discovered several supply chain attacks that compromised popular npm, PyPI and Cargo (the Rust package manager) packages. The malicious payloads in these packages targeted macOS systems along with others. For example, on July 11, an infected npm package, jscrambler, was published . Its malicious module was an infostealer written in Rust. The infostealer targeted crypto wallets, secrets from various services and browsers, MCP server configurations, and API keys for AI agents. In August, an attack was detected on the arrayref, internment, and append-only-vec Rust crates; it delivered a Rust backdoor to the victim’s device. In September, malicious versions of the MemTensor npm and PyPI packages were published . They delivered a Go backdoor that targeted secrets, configurations, and API tokens of various services. In August, Jamf researchers also reported discovering a new backdoor, Overlord . It was distributed as fake Zoom installers and had fairly broad spyware functionality, which is not often seen in macOS backdoors: it could eavesdrop through the microphone, watch the user through the camera, capture the screen, and log keystrokes. In the third quarter, we discovered an updated version of the MacSync crypto stealer and backdoor with a significantly changed payload delivery method. We’re also seeing more detections of the well-known Amos malware, both the traditional stealer and a version with backdoor functionality. articles.title: IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics
articles.raw_content:
IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Non-mobile statistics IT threat evolution in Q3 2026. Mobile statistics The mobile section of the quarterly cyberthreat report includes statistics on malware, adware, and potentially unwanted software for Android, as well as descriptions of the most notable threats for Android and iOS discovered during the reporting period. These statistics are based on detection alerts from Kaspersky products, collected from users who consented to provide statistical data to Kaspersky Security Network. The quarter in figures According to Kaspersky Security Network, in Q3 2026: More than 1.66 million attacks involving mobile malware, adware, or unwanted software were blocked. The Trojan-Banker category was the prevalent mobile malware threat with a 31.63% share of all detected malicious apps. Over 378,000 malicious installation packages were detected, including 119,688 mobile banking Trojan packages. Quarterly highlights In July, we discovered a malicious app targeting Brazilian users that may have used AI to automate fraud. The app was disguised as Google Play Protect, a suite of security services for Android devices. Malicious app imitating Google Play Protect The app’s code used the DistilBERT model to interpret natural-language commands sent from the C2 server. Traces left in the code suggest the server-side commands may also have been generated by a large language model (LLM). In August, we discovered a Trojan that analyzed images saved in the device’s gallery and took screenshots to look for banking data, including CVV codes. The malware used an on-device AI model to classify images. The app could also update this model, which gave the scammers a way to expand the Trojan’s functionality. In the third quarter, the infamous subscription Trojan detected as Trojan.AndroidOS.Subscriber.bh made it into Google Play again. This time, it was disguised as an app for creating keyboard themes. Subscription Trojan disguised as a keyboard theme app The Trojan opened a subscription link in a hidden WebView and intercepted the message containing the confirmation code. According to our data, the scammers mainly targeted users in Thailand. There were also new attacks on iOS users. In August, researchers at Socket discovered 13 infected PHP packages in the Packagist repository. The malicious payload injected links to fraudulent casinos into sites that used these packages and, on iOS devices only, a hidden iframe that loaded the DarkSword exploit kit. The attack delivered a spyware module that stole keychain contents, Wi-Fi passwords, SMS messages, photos, and other personal data. Other modules found in this campaign were used to steal crypto wallet data and the seed phrases used to recover them. SlowMist researchers found the same DarkSword exploit chain used in a fake app, FomoPeek. FomoPeek was published in the App Store, presenting itself as a crypto wallet tracker. The malware was designed to steal data from notes and crypto wallet apps. Also in August, we discovered infected versions of popular iOS apps distributed through Telegram (link in Russian). To install such an app, the attackers asked users to buy a developer certificate. The modified versions contained a malicious module that collected device information, took screenshots, and sent this data to a server. Mobile threat statistics The downward trend in attacks on mobile devices involving malware, adware, or unwanted software continued: the number fell to 1,668,368 in Q3 from 1,996,823 in Q2. Attacks on users of Kaspersky mobile solutions, Q1 2025 – Q3 2026 ( download ) In the third quarter, this decline was driven in part by fewer adware attacks, which we examine in more detail below. The number of Android malware samples grew compared to the previous reporting period, reaching 378,456. Detected malicious and potentially unwanted installation packages, Q3 2025 – Q3 2026 ( download ) The distribution of detected installation packages by type was as follows: Detected mobile apps by type, Q2*–Q3 2026 ( download ) * Data for the previous quarter may differ slightly from previously published data due to certain verdicts being retrospectively revised. The sharp rise in Trojan-Dropper apps comes from more droppers delivering known banking Trojans such as Mamont and Creduz. In the previous quarter, we described the trend of attackers “packaging” banking Trojans. The resulting malware is classified as droppers, which explains the growth. Note that standalone banking Trojans still rank first. Together with droppers, they account for more than half of all detected malicious apps. Share* of users attacked by the given type of malicious or potentially unwanted apps out of all targeted users of Kaspersky mobile products, Q2–Q3 2026 ( download ) * The total percentage may exceed 100% if the same users encountered multiple attack types. The number of AdWare.AndroidOS.HiddenAd and AdWare.AndroidOS.MobiDash attacks continued to decline, although adware traditionally ranks first by the number of attacked users. The growing share of Trojan-Dropper correlates with the increase in packaged banking Trojans described in the previous section. articles.title: Virtualization security: attack layers and misconfiguration impact
articles.raw_content:
Introduction Incidents in virtual environments can begin with a software vulnerability, human error, a configuration weakness, or several of these factors at once. The investigation is rarely limited to the workload. Hypervisors, container runtimes, management consoles, monitoring platforms, identity systems, virtual networks, datastores, backups, and automation accounts all influence what an attacker can reach. Kaspersky GERT recently investigated two more ransomware cases on ESXi and Proxmox environments in which weak access controls, insufficient network separation, exposed administrative services, and poor management of privileged credentials contributed to the impact. A monitoring system that could reach the virtualization layer also exposed a reusable root credential. Once the attacker controlled that route, ordinary administrative access was enough to affect several hosts. No VM escape was required. The incidents show why patching and secure configuration must be managed together. A fully patched hypervisor can still be compromised through a shared password, an overprivileged monitoring account, an open SSH path, or an administrator interface reachable from a general server network. NIST guidance places secure configuration baselines, restricted administrative access, current patches, and monitoring across all layers within the same set of sound security practices. In this article, we’re going to describe both incidents with additional focus on common unsafe practices that were exploited, leading to compromise, as well as remediation tactics. We’ll also discuss the broader scope of threats targeting virtual environments for a better understanding of possible protection strategies. The connected system defenders must protect A business virtual environment is not just Hyper-V, VMware, or Docker but rather a connected stack. Management consoles, orchestration tools, monitoring platforms, and automation accounts sit above hypervisors and container engines. Registries, image stores, virtual switches, datastores, and backup systems connect the layers. Applications and business services run at the bottom, while much of the administrative power sits near the top. The important boundaries extend beyond guest to host. They include workload to management plane, monitoring system to hypervisor, registry to deployment, administrator workstation to console, management plane to storage, and one virtual network segment to another. An attacker only needs one usable route. The possibility of compromise may lie in one stolen or insecurely placed administrator credential rather than in a complex escape exploit. In the GERT case, the compromise route passed through the monitoring platform and included a valid virtualization platform credential. Case #1: From network monitoring to ESXi encryption The investigation began with evidence of BlackNevas ransomware activity on a Windows system in a virtualized domain controller segment. UserAssist artifacts recorded execution of the AnyDesk RMM tool and GMER binaries. The environment also used PRTG Network Monitor to monitor its virtual infrastructure. UserAssist artifacts The available evidence showed that the PRTG deployment had broad access to the ESXi hosts and that the same root password was reused across several nodes. After obtaining access to the monitoring environment, the attacker used the ESXi credential to connect over SSH to the hosts that shared the same password. This design joined monitoring, credential storage, and direct administration into one attack path. PRTG supports storing VMware credentials at the device or inherited group level. That feature is operationally useful, but a monitoring server becomes privileged infrastructure when it holds credentials that can administer the systems it observes. The security question is therefore not whether monitoring needs access, but whether the identity, privileges, storage method, and permitted network path are limited to the monitoring task. The threat actor gained root access to the ESXi environment and used the esxcli command to bypass the system restriction by disabling the execInstalledOnly policy to execute the encryption binary and also perform anti-forensic log deletion. Let’s look closely at the timeline of the initial host compromise. ESXi (192.168.*.*) timeline 2025-10-18 Connection attempts from IP address 192.168.*.*.
2025-10-19 During an SSH session by root from IP 192.168.*.*, the file esx is uploaded to the system.
2025-10-19 User "root" attempts to execute the binary esx with the error "Execution of non-installed file prevented".
 chmod 777 esx
 ./esx /log
2025-10-19 User "root" deactivates the execInstalledOnly option.
 esxcli system settings advanced set -o 
 /User/execInstalledOnly -i 0
2025-10-19 User "root" executes the malware esx.
2025-10-19 New connection attempts from IP 192.168.*.*. Now, at the same time, the following activities ensued on a different host with the same password for the root user: ESXi (172.16.*.*) timeline 2025-10-19 SSH connection by user "root" from IP 172.16.*.*.
2025-10-19 User "root" executes the malware esx and clears the logs.
 chmod a+x esx && chmod 777 esx
 ./esx /selftest
 nohup ./esx /p /vmfs/ /depth 5 /log /wipe
 ./esx /depth 5 /log /wipe Case #2: Credential notes impacting the whole Proxmox environment GERT responded to a ransomware incident by The Gentlemen group, in which the threat actor gained access to Proxmox using information collected during the dwell time between initial access and visible impact. On a compromised system administrator workstation, the actor discovered administrative credentials and access details stored in notes in plain text. These records provided the information needed to log in to Proxmox using the root account. The actor then activated the VNC web socket through the compromised root account, gaining extensive control over the Proxmox environment. This access was subsequently used to download and execute ransomware within the cluster, which resulted in the encryption of the entire virtual environment. Below are the log records showing the root account being used to access other hosts via a VNC web socket. root@pam [01/08/2026:00:28:36 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=****
root@pam [01/08/2026:00:30:17 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=****
root@pam [01/08/2026:00:31:19 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=****
root@pam [01/08/2026:00:43:38 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=****
root@pam [01/08/2026:00:44:49 -0400] "GET /api2/json/nodes/******/vncwebsocket?port=5900&vncticket=**** This incident is a clear example of the risks of storing privileged credentials in unsecured notes or other easily accessible files. Once the administrator workstation was compromised, the saved credentials allowed the actor to move from a single endpoint into the virtualization management layer. Because the credentials belonged to a highly privileged root account, one poor credential handling practice significantly increased the scope and impact of the attack. Privileged credentials should instead be stored in an approved password manager or privileged access management system, protected with multifactor authentication and rotated immediately if an administrator workstation is suspected of being compromised. Why the misconfiguration caused broad impact Both cases exhibited unsafe misconfiguration practices whose exploitation led to a bigger impact on the host system. Next, we will break down each misconfiguration to see how it enabled further compromise and what should be done to avoid it. Monitoring inherited excessive privilege In Case 1, the monitoring platform could do more than collect health and performance data. It held or could use credentials with enough privilege to reach ESXi directly. A compromise of the monitoring system therefore became a compromise of the management plane. Monitoring identities should be dedicated to the task and given only the permissions required by the deployed sensors. Credential reuse Password reuse converted one recovered secret into farm-wide access. System administration should use named identities through the central management plane. Each host should have unique credentials and proper password storage hygiene. Password strength alone does not limit the impact of theft, but where the credential can be used and where it is stored do. Direct root access bypassed central control Direct SSH access allowed the actor to authenticate as root, upload a binary, and change a security setting without first passing through vCenter role controls. Broadcom, the parent company of VMware, recommends managing vSphere through vCenter, disabling SSH during normal operation, and using Lockdown Mode where suitable. Required service accounts should be explicit exceptions rather than members of a broad administrator group. Lack of enhanced security settings The initial execution attempt was blocked by execInstalledOnly , but the attacker had enough privilege to disable this policy. Broadcom documents enforcement options that combine execInstalledOnly with UEFI Secure Boot and TPM-backed configuration protection. These controls must be enabled, tested, and monitored for change. A setting that can be silently disabled by the same credential used for daily administration provides limited resistance after account compromise. Unsafe credential storage Case 2 demonstrated the possibility of compromise lying in privileged credential exposure. The mitigation strategy involves not only securing the administrative credential storage but also general hardening practices of secret handling, such as privilege management and regular access audits. How to close this attack path In this section, we share remediation advice on how to mitigate such attacks, and detect and prevent them from going further. We recommend the following actions: Separate monitoring from administration. Create a dedicated monitoring identity for each platform and restrict it to the smallest set of objects and actions that the monitoring sensors require. Do not use ESXi root or another emergency account for routine polling. Prevent monitoring servers from starting interactive administrator sessions unless a separately approved support workflow requires it. The same principle applies beyond VMware. Replace stored root passwords. Locate every copy of hypervisor, management, storage, and backup credentials in monitoring tools, scripts, scheduled tasks, connection managers, and service configurations. Replace static passwords with vault retrieval, brokered identities, or limited API tokens where the platform supports them. Record every retrieval and rotate the secret after emergency use or compromise. Restrict direct host access. Route normal ESXi administration through vCenter and enable an appropriate Lockdown Mode after testing monitoring, backup, and recovery dependencies. Keep ESXi Shell and SSH stopped by default. When support work requires SSH, enable it for a defined period, restrict the source, and alert on service activation, root login, and changes to the exception list of users who are allowed to connect via SSH. Use a specialized security solution. In our portfolio, Kaspersky Cloud Workload Security (KCWS) is perfectly suited to address virtual environment risks, offering a powerful combination of two products: Kaspersky Hybrid Cloud Security (KHCS) and Kaspersky Container Security (KCS). Kaspersky Hybrid Cloud Security is specifically built to secure virtualized infrastructures, private data centers, and hybrid clouds. A patented Light Agent architecture minimizes resource impact without compromising performance, while comprehensive infrastructure visualization through a unified console gives administrators complete visibility and control over the entire hybrid network. Kaspersky Container Security covers every stage of a containerized app’s lifecycle, from development to operation. Among other capabilities, the solution allows for detecting misconfigurations using a dedicated scanner for images, file systems, and repositories that contain IaC files (such as Terraform, CloudFormation, Azure ARM templates, Helm charts, and Dockerfiles). Treat configuration changes as security events. Alert when execInstalledOnly , Secure Boot enforcement, Lockdown Mode, SSH, local accounts, exception users, firewall rules, or remote logging settings change. Baseline the expected state and test whether the security team can detect an unauthorized change. A secure configuration set once does not mean that the control remains active on the host. Isolate the management network. Place hypervisor, monitoring, backup, storage, and cluster administration on restricted management networks. Permit only the exact source and destination services required. Administrative workstations should enter through hardened jump hosts with named identities and multifactor authentication. Protect logs, backups, and recovery. Forward ESXi, vCenter, Proxmox monitoring, identity, and network logs to protected storage that a compromised administrator cannot erase. Backup platforms should use separate identities, restricted management paths, and recovery copies outside ordinary administrative reach. Configuration checks for monitored virtualization Below are recommended checks to run when enabling virtualization monitoring. The safest state depends on the platform and monitoring method, but each control should be tested. Control area Safer state Verification Monitoring identity Dedicated service account or token with only required read and polling rights Review assigned roles and test every sensor without root or global administrator access Credential storage No recoverable host root password on a monitoring or general-purpose server Review tool configurations, scripts, scheduled tasks, and connection stores for embedded credentials, access tokens, or other secrets Network path Monitoring reaches only required polling services while administration uses a jump host Test management ports from monitoring server, user segments and untrusted network segments Direct host access Lockdown Mode where suitable with SSH and ESXi Shell stopped by default Attempt direct client API and SSH access to host using a routine account Configuration integrity Secure Boot and execInstalledOnly enforcement enabled where supported and tested Change a test setting through the approved process and confirm an alert is generated Evidence Host, management, identity, monitoring, firewall, and PAM logs stored remotely Generate successful and failed logins and verify source, account, host, time, and action The wider attack surface Closing the monitoring and credential routes does not secure the environment by itself. Virtualization also relies on isolation boundaries, trusted images, management APIs, virtual networks, storage, and backups. Each layer requires a different control and leaves evidence in a different place. VM and container escapes In a VM escape, code inside a guest reaches past the VM boundary and affects the host or another guest. The weakness may be in a virtual device, an integration feature, a hypercall interface, or another component that translates guest requests for the host. If the escape works, control of one VM may lead to control of the physical server and every workload on it. VMware CVE-2025-22224 showed this risk: an attacker with administrator rights inside a VM could execute code as the VMX process on the host, and Broadcom reported exploitation in the wild. A container escape can reach a similar result, but the starting point is different. Linux containers share the host kernel, so their isolation model differs from that of a VM. Namespaces limit what processes can see, cgroups control resource use, and capabilities split root privileges into smaller parts. A kernel or runtime bug can break this isolation. Copy Fail (CVE-2026-31431) is a good example of a kernel flaw. Code already running in a container could use a Linux AF_ALG crypto socket to change pages in the shared Linux kernel page cache. Because the host and other containers may read the same cached pages, the effect did not have to stay inside one container. The fix is a kernel update; Docker Engine 29.4.3 also tightened its default security profiles to reduce exposure on hosts that had not yet been patched. Unsafe settings can also break the boundary. Privileged mode, excessive capabilities, writable host mounts, or access to the Docker socket may remove isolation without any software exploit. For instance, runc CVE-2024-21626 involved leaked file descriptors that could expose the host filesystem to a malicious image or container process. This difference changes the investigation. A VM can often be treated like a separate computer with its own kernel, memory, and disk. A container is a group of host processes placed inside namespaces. If investigators collect only the container filesystem, they may leave the most useful process, socket, and control-plane evidence on the host. Images and templates A compromised golden VM image or container base image can spread through normal automation. Common weaknesses include unofficial public images, mutable tags, overprivileged build tokens, recoverable secrets in older layers, and stale templates that restore vulnerable software or forgotten accounts. Scanning might help, but it does not establish who built the artifact or whether the exact image tested and approved was the one ultimately deployed to production. Use controlled builders, provenance records, signature checks, and planned rebuilds from trusted sources. Management tools and APIs A stolen vCenter identity, exposed Docker API, overpowered Portainer role, or compromised backup console may give an attacker an easier route than an escape exploit. Portainer advisory GHSA-7fw3-x4r2-g7wc showed how a proxy validated one bind-mount representation but missed an equivalent API form, allowing an authenticated non-administrator with container creation privileges to reach host paths. The runtime performed a valid request after authorization had already failed in the management layer. Administrative file-copy operations also deserve attention. Docker fixed archive and mount-handling flaws in CVE-2026-41567, CVE-2026-41568, and CVE-2026-42306. These cases required particular conditions and operator or API activity. They are a reminder to patch the daemon and record who initiated copy operations, which container was involved, the source and destination paths, and the result. Virtual networks, storage, and backups East-west traffic between virtual workloads may stay inside one host and bypass a physical sensor. Management, migration, storage, and workload traffic should use separate zones with filtering between them. Snapshot and memory files may contain credentials, while weak datastore permissions can expose whole virtual disks. Backup systems need broad access to recover services, which also makes them valuable to an attacker who wants to delete recovery points or reach several hosts. Attack surface examples by layer To sum up, the described attack vectors might be mitigated as follows: Attack surface Initial access Possible impact Primary control Credentials and configuration Password recovered from monitoring or an overprivileged account Direct control of several hypervisor nodes Unique vaulted credentials, segmented access, and configuration monitoring VM escape Administrative access or code execution privileges inside a guest plus a hypervisor flaw Host process or neighboring workload compromise Patch the hypervisor and reduce risky virtual devices and guest privilege Malicious container affecting kernel or runtime Code in a container or a malicious image Host filesystem, kernel, or shared cache impact Patch kernel and runtime, and remove privileged settings Images and templates Compromised build input registry or golden image Repeated deployment of the compromise Immutable digests, controlled builds, provenance, and verification Management API Stolen identity exposing endpoint or authorization gap Fleet-wide administrative actions MFA, least privilege, network restrictions, and complete API validation Networks, storage, and backups Flat network or broad datastore and access through backups Lateral movement, data theft, encryption, and recovery loss Segmentation, least privilege, protected backups, and traffic monitoring Conclusion GERT cases that we presented in this article did not require an attacker to break the VM boundary. The attack path was created by an overprivileged monitoring relationship, an insecure password storage approach, a recoverable and reused root credential, broad management-network reachability, and direct SSH administration. Each element was legitimate on its own, but together they allowed one compromise to reach virtualization hosts and their workloads. Misconfiguration should therefore receive the same operational attention as vulnerability management. Teams need to know where privileged credentials exist, which systems can use them, which network paths make them effective, and which logs will show their use. Escape flaws, unsafe images, API weaknesses, virtual network exposure, and attacks on storage or backups remain serious, but closing the known administrative route should come first.

A detailed breakdown of misconfigurations in virtual environment cybersecurity as shown by examples of ransomware cases on ESXi and Proxmox environments.

articles.title: The SOC Files 5: Ghost in the pipeline, or a fileless SharePoint breach by Storm-2603
articles.raw_content:
Table of Contents

Executive summary

Intrusion timeline: Strategic latency and exploitation

Initial access validation phase

Vulnerability fingerprinting

Active exploitation: Santa took your data and left a backdoor

Attack originated from an SPN node

Webshell architecture

“G.cs” pipeline control and C2

Pipeline control

Command and control layer (in-memory transport)

“Prog.cs”: Execution entry point and task dispatcher

Host interaction modules

“FileDownloader.cs”

“LoggedOnUsers.cs”

“ProcessList.cs”

“NetworkInfo.cs”

Privilege escalation

Post-exploitation activity

EDR-killing attempts

Ransomware deployment attempt

What defenders really need to look for

ToolPane deserialization and CLR artifacts

Detecting deserialization exploitation

Detecting a VPP-based webshell/runtime implant

Indicator of compromise

Alexander Rodchenko

Rodrigo Wanderson

In 2025, several threat actors exploited CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771 (ToolShell vulnerabilities) in on-premises Microsoft SharePoint to achieve remote code execution through crafted HTTP requests. One of the threat actors deployed ransomware on the target’s systems after successful exploitation. Microsoft attributed this ransomware-related ToolShell activity to Storm-2603, distinguishing it from other actors whose observed activity was primarily focused on credential theft, espionage, and data exfiltration.

In December, our retrospective analysis identified activity consistent with Storm-2603’s TTPs. This activity involved the attacker using the IIS worker process as an in-memory bridge to the customer’s infrastructure, keeping the access and control layer entirely within w3wp.exe without writing anything to disk. Although subsequent post-exploitation activity generated disk artifacts, the bridge used to maintain access remained memory-resident.

Let’s look in more detail at this attack.

The attack chain, from reconnaissance to infrastructure compromise

The intrusion analyzed in this report occurred in two stages, with a temporal gap between initial access and subsequent exploitation activity. The attack timeline was as follows:

Dec 20 – Vulnerability fingerprinting: A single HTTP request targeted a SharePoint administrative endpoint associated with the ToolPane component to determine whether the host was vulnerable to CVE-2025-53770.

Dec 21-23 – Tactical latency: A three-day period of silence followed the initial probe, separating the vulnerability fingerprinting from subsequent malicious activity and potentially reducing the likelihood of immediate detection.

Dec 24 – High-intensity re-engagement: On Christmas Eve, when security staffing at many companies is reduced, the full RCE chain was executed through the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) on the same endpoint as the initial probe.

Dec 26 – Incident discovery: The three-day gap initially prevented the December 20 probe from being correlated with subsequent malicious activity, marking the event as low priority. Retrospective analysis established that the probe was the initial phase of the subsequent intrusion.

Intrusion timeline

A vulnerability fingerprinting request on December 20 marked the first observed interaction with the target. The request originated from infrastructure associated with ONYPHE, an internet-scale attack surface discovery and management platform for identifying exposed assets, vulnerabilities, and cyberthreats. Unlike widely used tools such as Shodan and Censys, which merely provide a list of internet-facing assets correlated with the open-source data about known vulnerabilities, ONYPHE actually checks if the target system is vulnerable.

Fingerprinting with ONYPHE

The request characteristics were consistent with ONYPHE’s vulnerability checks, which use active, non-intrusive probes to identify internet-exposed systems vulnerable to specific CVEs. For ToolShell, ONYPHE adopted the approach used by Niels Hofmans (hazcod). Namely, it attempts to inject a harmless marker into the target server to find out if it is vulnerable.

OFFICIAL ONYPHE CVE CHECKER (TOOLSHELL)

This phase served as a validation step against the SharePoint execution surface exposed over HTTP:

The target processed structured requests through the ASP.NET pipeline without rejection.

The request path reached application logic capable of handling serialized input.

No defensive controls interrupted or altered the execution flow at the application boundary.

Approximately 12 minutes later, a second inbound connection originated from infrastructure associated with Pfcloud UG, a provider operating under a bulletproof hosting (BPH) model. Given the timing and the IP’s documented history of scanning and abusive activity, the connection may represent follow-on reconnaissance against the newly identified target. No exploitation was attempted at this stage.

A connection from an IP address belonging to Pfcloud UG BPH

The main malicious activity occurred on December 24. The actor targeted the same SharePoint host with a crafted request from 45.91.94.204 (45.91.92.0/22, ASN 63473, HostHatch, LLC). This resulted in a webshell execution within the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe). The payload was not written to disk; rather, it was loaded directly into the ASP.NET runtime and used during subsequent request processing. The implant remained resident for the lifetime of the affected application domain. This runtime state was lost when the application pool was recycled or IIS was restarted.

The IP address 45.91.94.204 is a Safing Privacy Network (SPN) node. SPN routes each connection through a multilayer VPN path with multiple relay nodes that can obscure the originating IP.

SPN promotes itself as a network that offers strong privacy protection for internet traffic. Its infrastructure resembles Tor’s in many ways, but with some differences. It features the following capabilities:

Speed: Near-VPN performance for high-speed data transfer.

Layer 3 support: Supports multiple protocols like TCP, UDP, ICMP (unlike Tor, which only supports TCP).

App-routing: Direct tunneling without a browser.

Multi-identity: Simultaneous exit nodes to bypass IP rate limits.

Fixed-size packets and padding make it harder to analyze its traffic.

It is less common than Tor, and frequently bypasses standard Tor blocklists.

The webshell the attackers injected into the w3wp.exe runtime is a multi-module in-memory framework, where execution is orchestrated through the main component (G.cs) and extended via multiple functional units across namespaces.

The implementation follows a modular C# project structure in which each capability is isolated into its own compilation unit and invoked dynamically at runtime.

Webshell components

The main webshell component is G.cs. It orchestrates the implant’s execution context, lifecycle, C2 and session management.

To ensure persistence within the runtime, G.cs performs the following actions:

Registers a custom VirtualPathProvider using the non-public RegisterVirtualPassProviderInternal method from the ASP.NET HostingEnvironment class so that ASP.NET uses it for virtual-path processing. The provider is automatically added to the chain of registered virtual path providers.

VirtualPathProvider

RegisterVirtualPassProviderInternal

HostingEnvironment

Delegates the provider’s .NET Remoting lifetime policy to the previous provider in the chain, preserving the existing lifetime behavior.

Additionally, to evade defenses and enable the VirtualPathProvider to be registered even if the application in whose AppDomain the webshell is running is precompiled, the module implements the trust control subversion (T1553) technique:

VirtualPathProvider

Uses reflection to check if the application is precompiled.

Extracts pointers for internal state fields for the BuildManager class, which manages application compilation, and modifies them at runtime.

Uses reflection once again to force runtime injection.

G.cs uses the GetCacheKey() function as the interception point for the virtual path processing flow. It processes incoming requests to the SharePoint server and checks their headers to filter out requests from the attacker.

The specific User-Agent in the request headers triggers the webshell execution. If the request doesn’t match this condition, the implant remains dormant, making its traffic harder to recognize.

The same core module (G.cs) implements the communication layer.

Instead of relying on external frameworks or standard beacons, it uses a custom binary protocol with XOR-based obfuscation to exchange data with the C2. These communications blend into normal application traffic. The module uses the GetCacheKey() hook to intercept standard HTTP requests. When a specific User-Agent is detected in the request headers, the module parses it, extracts the payload, and establishes a TCP connection to a target host inside the target’s network if needed.

Bidirectional TCP tunnel initialization

G.cs establishes a full-duplex proxy tunnel to support interactive control. It stores active target sockets in memory to pair concurrent HTTP read and write channels.

TCP connections from the C2 server to arbitrary hosts inside the target network are supported for pivoting and lateral movement. The traffic is proxied through the SharePoint host.

Target-to-attacker data channel

Attacker-to-target data channel

As can be seen in the screenshots, the attackers used the suo5 tool to implement traffic proxying. Its authors promote it as a stable forward-proxying tool for scenarios where outbound internet connections are prohibited.

To increase its performance, G.cs manipulates ThreadPool by raising its limits for concurrent operations and maximum timeout.

ThreadPool manipulation

Prog.cs is the entry point that receives command-line arguments and passes them to uk/London.cs. The latter acts as the orchestrator, handling command parsing and privilege escalation (via named pipe impersonation). We’ll review it in more detail later. If the “suo5” command is provided, London.cs triggers G.cs to hook into the ASP.NET runtime as a memory shell. Once active, G.cs independently processes incoming web traffic inside the web server memory.

The following modules provide direct system interaction capabilities, each implemented as a separate unit. London.cs triggers these modules when it receives a corresponding command from Prog.cs.

The FileDownloader.cs module downloads arbitrary files from external URLs provided by the C2. It stores the downloaded files in the Program Data directory without any user interaction.

This module enumerates logged-on users and identifies their session types (interactive, service, remote). The results are stored in memory. The attackers can retrieve them using the proxy and tunneling capabilities provided by G.cs.

This module lists running processes with full paths to the corresponding executables on the disk. The results are stored in memory and the attackers can retrieve them via G.cs.

This module extracts information about existing network connections, including protocols, local and remote IPs and ports, and connection state. It also enumerates network interfaces and headers. The results are stored in memory and can be retrieved by the attackers via G.cs.

This module silently installs and executes MSI packages previously downloaded by FileDownloader.cs.

This module creates administrative accounts using the native SAM RPC subsystem (SAMRPCNative namespace) rather than standard command-line tooling. This may indicate an attempt to evade detection and provide the attackers with privileged stealthy access to target systems that persists after the webshell has finished its work.

The SAMRPCNative namespace implements a low-level C# P/Invoke wrapper for the native Windows samlib.dll library, comprising three types: SAMStructs.cs, SAMMethods.cs, and SAMEnums.cs.

Implements structured bitwise lists and constant flags mapping numeric codes to their security meaning in SAM, and translates system status return codes.

Defines native data structures required for P/Invoke memory alignment and for marshalling. It securely formats and aligns data structures.

Contains external API declarations (P/Invoke) imported from samlib.dll to perform actions such as connecting to the SAM server, creating users and opening domains.

This layer is crucial for the attackers because it enables account operations.

The uk namespace contains offensive primitives for privilege escalation. To elevate privileges to SYSTEM, it uses a local token impersonation technique via the Encrypting File System Remote Protocol (EFSRPC) interface adopted from the EfsPotato tool.

This functionality is implemented in the uk/London class. It creates a malicious named pipe while the EfsrTiny class (a tiny version of the EfsPotato tool) connects to the LSASS.exe RPC server. Then it’s London.RpcThread function calls the EfsRpcEncryptFileSrv function from EfsrTiny with a crafted \\localhost path. This tricks LSASS.exe into connecting back to the attacker’s named pipe. Finally, the London.Exp function uses ImpersonateNamedPipeClient to coerce and impersonate the LSASS.exe token and spawn a new process via CreateProcessAsUser with SYSTEM privileges. As the webshell resides in the IIS worker process, it has the necessary SeImpersonatePrivilege to perform this technique.

London.RpcThread

EfsRpcEncryptFileSrv

ImpersonateNamedPipeClient

CreateProcessAsUser

SeImpersonatePrivilege

The uk namespace also implements a minimal MSRPC client layer by explicitly defining structures such as RPC_CLIENT_INTERFACE and MIDL_STUB_DESC , thereby spoofing an interface stub. This enables direct interaction with the Windows RPC runtime (Rpcrt4.dll) without relying on MIDL-generated stubs or higher-level RPC abstractions. This provides direct control over binding and marshaling that goes beyond the constraints of standard client APIs.

RPC_CLIENT_INTERFACE

Shortly after the webshell injection, the infected worker process spawned msiexec.exe to install a remote MSI payload hosted in Supabase cloud storage. The payload was Velociraptor, an open-source digital forensics and incident response tool – namely version 0.73.4.0 vulnerable to CVE-2025-6264 – that the attackers abused for command execution on the target network.

In October 2025, Cisco Talos reported Velociraptor being leveraged by threat actors as a post-compromise execution framework and attributed this activity to Storm-2603. This tool enables arbitrary command execution, and can be used for various purposes. In our case, it was used for persistence, discovery, data collection and payload execution.

The threat actor used Velociraptor to deploy multiple independent tunneling mechanisms, including Zoho Assist-Unattended Support for unauthorized remote access, VS Code CLI tunneling, Cloudflare Tunnel, and a lightweight reverse proxy utility. By doing so, they attempted to maintain access even if some of their tools were detected and deleted. At this stage, they also no longer depended on the IIS worker process lifecycle and ToolShell vulnerability.

Once the threat actor had access to the target system, they were able to upload a vulnerable driver that is used by many attackers to terminate EDR solutions. We were able to detect the main driver at C:\programdata\rsndispot.sys (054a32d6033b1744dca7f49b2e466ea2). In addition, the adversary used a malicious DLL (2d9ebf9c042f596f435865b40edad928) in a sideloading attack. This DLL was identified as Warlock ransomware’s AV killer. It was possibly intended to kill security solutions using the vulnerable rsndispot.sys driver.

The attackers made attempts to launch ransomware on the compromised system. However, the Proactive Defense Module in Kaspersky Endpoint Security blocked the ransomware process, effectively preventing this activity. The malware DLL we obtained was identified as Warlock ransomware.
