articles.title: MLEP in KICS for Networks 5.0: how machine learning helps track network behavior of OT devices
articles.raw_content:
In an industrial network, malicious activity can be hard to tell apart from normal data exchange between devices. Malicious actors routinely rely on legitimate tools and the Living-off-the-Land technique, so a single network connection may show no known signs of an attack: the device uses a familiar protocol and transmits ordinary data. An anomaly can hide in subtle details: the data source, the time of access, or the volume of transferred data may be atypical for a particular device. However, to detect this kind of anomaly, you need to understand the roles of the devices at both ends of the connection and know which network activity patterns are typical for them. But an organization’s asset inventory data is often incomplete, which makes it harder to catch unauthorized connections in time. Suppose monitoring detects a host that regularly exchanges data with programmable logic controllers (PLCs). Its IP address is known, but the inventory does not specify what role it plays: is it an engineering workstation, a process data server, or a piece of contractor’s equipment? The host may also have been on the industrial network for a long time, with its record going out of date after a network upgrade. In the joint OT asset inventory guidance released by CISA and its partners in 2025 , inventorying devices and classifying them by role are treated as part of OT asset management. For organizations, this is one of the most important areas: according to the SANS 2025 ICS security survey , 50% of respondents had deployed or significantly expanded ICS inventory and visibility tools over the previous 12 months, and 54% named them as investment priorities for the next 12–24 months. Device inventory in Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks In Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks , the Asset Discovery technology is the foundation of asset visibility. Passive network traffic analysis detects devices and their interactions, while recognition rules help determine the device category and extract available information about it, such as the vendor, model, or software version. Exactly which attributes the system can obtain depends on the protocol and the traffic it observes. We covered this in more detail at the Kaspersky Industrial Cybersecurity Conference . Hardware and software information in the device card The product also supports active polling modules (APMs): where polling is allowed, they can request additional configuration and firmware version details from devices. This kind of inventory is far more detailed than a list of IP addresses. Installed modules and their placement in a PLC rack However, even accurate hardware information doesn’t always explain what function a host performs in a specific industrial facility. Gaps appear for various reasons. Some devices send identifying information only at startup or during configuration, while others rarely communicate. Proprietary protocols can’t always be parsed, and encryption may leave only connection metadata for analysis. If the monitoring system doesn’t receive traffic from every segment of the industrial network, some network activity goes unobserved. Active polling doesn’t suit every device or every operating condition. Devices of unknown category When there isn’t enough direct information about a device, its category can be refined by looking at the patterns of its recurring network interactions. Analyzing these interactions is the job of Machine Learning Event Processor (MLEP), a service included in Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks 5.0. This machine-learning-based event processor can both refine device categories and detect anomalies in their network behavior. What data does MLEP analyze? To compare device behavior, you don’t need to store every packet as a separate observation (a data object) in the ML model. MLEP represents network sessions as a sequence of short 15-second fragments. For each fragment, MLEP stores information about the endpoints (IP, MAC, and port), the direction of data exchange, the protocol, and the number and size of the packets transmitted. Together these make up an event , which then gets a timestamp. Traffic thus becomes a sequence of events showing which hosts a device communicated with, when, and how communication intensity changed. Aggregating data into events also sets the method’s limits. An aggregated fragment can’t be used to reconstruct the exact order of individual packets or the content of commands. MLEP can draw conclusions about a new protocol only if another KICS technology has managed to recognize it. That said, comparing stable network connections and changes in exchange volume doesn’t require a detailed record of every packet. These observations form the basis of the device’s behavioral history. From observations to MLEP results Each object has its own behavioral history, and one object’s history can’t be applied to another. But the principles of behavior analysis, along with some common rules, work across different objects. Let’s look at how this works in MLEP, which is built on a spiking neural semantic network (NSN). Event identification Neurosemantic networks structure information as a multilayer ordered graph, where the data in each consecutive layer builds on the data in the previous one. The nodes of this graph — that is, the units of information in each layer — act as neurons.The NSN creates dedicated channels to handle different event parameters (port, IP, and so on). Unique parameter values for each channel are stored as neurons in layer 0. The event itself, which consists of a set of parameter values, is stored as a neuron in layer 1 of the network. If an event occurs for the first time, neurogenesis creates a new neuron with input connections to the corresponding parameter neurons. This lets the network learn and operate on the event stream at the same time. If the event has occurred before, the network activates the same neuron that was created when the event first appeared. This way, the network identifies each event precisely. Each neuron that corresponds to an event also collects basic statistics: when it was last activated and how many times it has been activated. Event history In NSN-based event processing, layer 2 and above store sequences of events over time: recurring patterns and the full history. However, categorization and statistical anomaly detection don’t require storing the full packet sequence or a detailed timeline of every network event. As we noted earlier, events are themselves aggregates, which means the order of network packets has already been averaged out. So MLEP keeps history only temporarily, within each episode (30,000 aggregated events by default), which saves computing resources. Statistics processing in MLEP MLEP processes statistics mainly through specialized listener neurons on layer −1 (minus one) of the network. Attention heads and monitors are built on these neurons. Key components of the NSN When an event arrives, the corresponding neuron is activated, and the network instantly knows whether that neuron is new or was created earlier. Each attention head subscribes to the events or event features it needs and takes in only the activations of the matching neurons. If an event occurs for the first time, all heads are notified and then decide whether to subscribe (grow a connection to the relevant neuron) and receive information about activations of such neurons from then on. It is called a spiking network because activation information is a spike, not a number. This spike tells the head that something it’s interested in has happened. An attention head is configured according to scenarios — the situations that MLEP should send alerts about. The core of a head’s configuration is a query, which filters incoming information and serves as the subscription criterion. Unlike regular database queries, this query runs on the stream, so it can react to an event instantly. Attention heads work very much like the semantics of ordinary human language. A query has a subject of attention (one or more grammatical subjects) and conditions (the other parts of the sentence). In the infrastructure of an industrial enterprise, the subjects are devices on the network, and the conditions are various aspects of network communication, such as ports, protocol, and average packet size. If a head has many subjects (for example, if it’s interested in every device on an industrial network), it fans out: it creates a child head for each individual value of the subject of attention, that is, each device. The child head then watches a specific device and reports to the parent head. Attention heads don’t accumulate or process statistics. They only filter event streams. When an attention head receives a relevant event, it activates and sends a spike to the monitor subscribed to that head. Monitors, in turn, have stacks for accumulating and processing events. They can also have their own queries and post-filter information from the head. For example, they can select only new events from those filtered by the head. There are several types of monitors: Stat monitors track changes in the average count of specific events (for example, device activity) over time intervals typical for those events, or in the average values of numeric event parameters (for example, changes in device traffic volume). Monitors work from the event alone: they fire when an event has occurred a certain number of times within a given interval, or has occurred for the first time. Similar-behavior monitors work with heads that can generalize events, that is, extract just a few parameters whose combination is shared (generalized) across many events. MLEP uses these monitor types to implement scenarios for categorizing devices and detecting their anomalous behavior: For categorization, MLEP uses attention heads and monitors that identify common behavior across different assets and group devices accordingly. MLEP then takes information from Asset Discovery about the known categories of some assets and extends those categories to other assets in the same group. Because a device can show different types of activity, it may land in several groups. MLEP then makes a weighted assessment across all relevant groups. Groups of devices with similar network behavior At the final stage, the system verifies that assigning the category to the asset is permissible. This is again done by special rule monitors loaded into the NSN at system startup. The rules rely on asset metadata available from Asset Discovery and APMs. MLEP takes a similar approach to anomaly detection: an attention head and a monitor define an anomaly scenario, often loosely. When a monitor activates on such a scenario, MLEP generates an alert about unusual behavior. The current version of MLEP ships with preconfigured heads and monitors. The functional dynamic diagram below shows how events from devices on an industrial network are processed. Event processing flow (click to play) MLEP in practice: how behavior helps complete the asset inventory At a facility with several similar production lines, device information may be more complete on some lines than on others. On one line, devices are identified as PLCs, while on another, after an upgrade, some hosts show up only as addresses: the available traffic didn’t provide enough information to determine their category. Still, these devices communicate with the same types of HMIs and process data collection servers. Their communication directions, frequency, and volumes may be similar. That’s where MLEP comes in. It takes the categories of already known assets and matches recurring features of their network behavior against those of uncategorized devices. When the observed interactions turn out to be similar, MLEP can add a category for that host to the inventory. Device category suggested by MLEP Once the category is refined, the industrial network map provides more context about the equipment on the network. When analyzing network activity, the analyst immediately sees the device’s suggested category and can skip looking up each IP address in the design diagrams. This approach is especially useful where equipment changes faster than the documentation is updated. The suggested category is also checked against existing device information and defined constraints. This helps filter out some contradictory options, but prediction quality still depends on how much of the traffic is visible, especially if the device communicates only rarely. Anomalous activity and streaming statistics Investigations of real-world attacks show that attackers actively use both standard tools and permitted protocols. You don’t always need to know an attacker’s specific technique in advance to spot potentially malicious activity. Signature-based detection helps find known signs of an attack, but it doesn’t assess how typical an observed interaction is for a particular device. MLEP compares current activity with the device’s usual network profile: which hosts it communicates with, which protocols it uses, when and how much data it transmits, its average packet size, and so on. The changes it detects help guide the direction of the investigation. Correlating these changes with other events and the operational context helps determine whether malicious actions could be behind them. When investigating an incident that has already been detected, anomalies help reconstruct the sequence of actions. The first version of MLEP comes with six preconfigured monitors, one for each type of deviation from the device’s usual network profile: Anomaly How it helps with event analysis New external host Flags a new external connection that wasn’t previously seen in the device’s observed behavior, even if the IP address isn’t listed among known IoCs. Helps check whether this connection appeared at the same time as other suspicious events. New combination of destination address and port Shows that the device has begun using a service it hasn’t used before. Once an incident has been detected, this helps trace new connections after the more critical events have been analyzed. Unusually large volume of data sent Highlights data transfers that are atypical for the device and helps correlate their timing and direction with other events. Atypical activity time Shows that the device was active at a time that’s unusual for it. In an already detected incident, this helps reconstruct the timeline of actions around the main alert. New protocol Helps spot a new method of communication, even when the device is communicating with familiar hosts. Activity with signs of scanning Shows that the device has started contacting an unusually large number of neighboring hosts. This signal helps reveal possible reconnaissance ahead of attempts to access equipment. During an investigation, anomalies help reconstruct the sequence of changes: when a specific host established new connections, switched protocols, increased its data transfer volume, or shifted its operating hours. Matching events by device and time shows an analyst how activity unfolded around an incident that has already been detected. This is especially useful when some of the attacker’s actions fell outside the monitored scope or didn’t trigger other KICS technologies. Correlating these changes with the device’s role, protocol analysis data, and events from other technologies gives the analyst a more complete timeline. Behavioral anomalies show exactly where to look for the missing links and which network interactions need attention. Atypical Activity Time anomaly card In the event list, anomalies detected by MLEP are marked with an AI label. Each event shows its name, source, destination, timestamp, and the ID of the triggered scenario. Conclusion In an industrial network, whether behavior is anomalous depends on the host where it occurs and that host’s place in the industrial process. The repetitive nature of many communications makes a change in normal data exchange easier to spot, while knowing a device’s function and criticality helps gauge the possible consequences. Taken together, these observations make network traffic more than a list of connections: it helps assess new events in the context of a specific facility, even without an attack scenario known in advance. Machine learning technologies are well suited to this kind of comprehensive analysis, as they can process and organize huge streams of heterogeneous data. Starting with version 5.0, Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks handles this function with MLEP, which works effectively alongside the product’s existing functionality.

We explain how Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks uses Machine Learning Event Processor (MLEP) technology to help take inventory of assets and detect anomalies in industrial networks.

articles.title: CyberStrikeAI in the wild: the use of AI in real-world attacks on organizations
articles.raw_content:
Table of Contents

Timeline of the attack

Technical details

CyberStrikeAI overview

Execution & Privilege Escalation

Remote Discovery

Domain Discovery

Credential Access

Lateral Movement

Command & Control

Collection & Exfiltration

Detection by Kaspersky solutions

Indicators of compromise

As part of proactive threat monitoring, Kaspersky’s Cyber Threat Intelligence team identified a malicious campaign involving C2 agents controlled by artificial intelligence. Confirmed victims of the campaign included organizations in the education sector in several countries across Africa and Latin America. CyberStrikeAI played a key role in the post-exploitation phase. This is an open-source framework in which an LLM orchestrator on the command-and-control server plans actions, selects tools, and generates commands, while an implant executes them on compromised hosts. Using CyberStrikeAI, the attackers progressed from reconnaissance to full domain compromise.

According to our data, this is one of the first public descriptions of a compromise involving an LLM in the wild. The campaign we discovered clearly illustrates how the role of AI in attackers’ arsenals is evolving: until recently, language models were used primarily during preparatory stages – for writing phishing emails, debugging code, or searching for vulnerabilities. Now, however, they are being embedded into the very core of the attack, automating actions at every stage: payload execution, persistence on the host, discovery, lateral movement, and, finally, data collection and exfiltration. Post-exploitation – the stage that traditionally required manual work by an experienced operator – plays a particularly significant role here.

A key feature of the scheme using the CyberStrikeAI framework is that the implant ceases to be a simple tool for executing the operator’s commands. Decisions are distributed across two levels: the operator defines the task in general terms, while the model determines how to execute it – specifically, which commands to send to the host and in what sequence. Thus, the strategic planning remains with the human, while the choice of technical steps is delegated to the model, and the implant executes the model’s decisions.

To understand how this scheme works in practice, let’s examine the chain of actions taken by the attackers, as reconstructed by our analysts during the incident investigation.

Let’s examine the timeline of the attack using an example from one incident within the detected campaign.

The first phase follows a standard approach: a human operator gains access to the victim’s infrastructure via a compromised SQL Server (version 16.0.1000), then collects basic information about the host, deploys tools, and conducts network reconnaissance. All of this activity takes nearly a day, followed by a two-week pause.

The second phase is fundamentally different. The first step involves deploying the CyberStrikeAI C2 agent, which receives commands from a server-based LLM orchestrator. During the second phase, the agent performs the following:

establishing persistence and conducting local reconnaissance within 2 minutes;

conducting domain reconnaissance over the next 5 hours;

after a brief pause of several days, moving on to the final stage – lateral movement via SMB and WMI, mass credential dumping on hosts, and database export – with the entire operation taking no more than one hour.

We’ll discuss these stages in more detail in the next section.

CyberStrikeAI is an open-source, modular platform written in Go for automating penetration testing. Its key feature is combining LLM-based attack orchestration and a built-in C2 server with agents (beacons) within a single server process.

The entire “intelligent” layer is isolated on the control server. C2 functions (calling reconnaissance and exploitation utilities, managing webshell connections, assigning tasks to agents, and reading results) are available to the model as MCP tools. The implant is a classic C2 agent with no AI functionality – no API keys, no calls to AI service APIs, and no autonomous logic. It periodically polls the listener server via HTTP/S, TCP, or WebSocket, executes shell commands, and interacts with the file system. To the victim, this activity looks like a typical remote-control session, where a server-side LLM orchestrator queues tasks instead of a live operator. The LLM influences how decisions are made, but not how the corresponding commands are delivered to the host.

Although CyberStrikeAI is publicly available, specific instances of the framework can be linked to specific attackers or campaigns. Detection and attribution are possible based on the following artifacts:

Control panel : Upon launch, a self-signed TLS certificate is generated, with the framework’s name appearing in the issuer and subject fields. The certificate is created in memory at each startup, so the not_before field effectively records the time the process was launched. Accordingly, as with Cobalt Strike, the chronology of restarts can be reconstructed from the scan history. CyberStrikeAI control panel’s self-signed TLS certificate

CyberStrikeAI control panel’s self-signed TLS certificate

CyberStrikeAI control panel’s self-signed TLS certificate

Implant : The build metadata ( go version -m ) contains a path to the main package, which includes data pointing to the built-in CyberStrikeAI generator – a temporary directory with the build identifier. This path is identical for all payloads, making it a reliable signature. Additionally, the build info field contains version control system metadata, which can be used to compare samples against one another.

Authentication : When communicating with the server, the implant sends an X-Implant-Token header with a fixed value in the HTTP request. The token is unique to each C2 server and is embedded into the malicious payload during the build phase; therefore, it serves as both a network indicator and a sign that the samples belong to the same server.

HTTP header parameters sent by the implant to the server

It should be noted that the implant version does not reflect the server version. The implant can operate for months while the operator updates the server-side components: listener configurations and keys are preserved during updates. In the incidents we detected, we observed the use of a single agent version throughout the entire incident. In such cases, the sample’s build date may indicate the earliest possible deployment date of the CyberStrikeAI infrastructure, but it still does not provide an estimate of the compromise duration.

The first malicious commands on the victims’ systems in the campaign under investigation originated from the sqlservr.exe process, indicating the likely initial access vector and the context in which the attackers gained the ability to execute code. It is important to note that the commands marked as having been executed prior to agent installation were executed manually by the attacker specifically within the context of this process. At this stage, we are not yet dealing with automated implant activity, but rather with manual actions by the operator.

Before launching the agent on the machines, the attackers checked for its presence using a PowerShell script, from which we can deduce its default deployment paths: C:\Windows\Temp\, C:\Windows\, C:\ProgramData\, C:\Temp. At the same time, the attacker can disguise the agent’s name as that of a legitimate system process. In the example below, it mimics svchost.exe (svchost s .exe)

Checking for the presence of the CyberStrikeAI agent on the system

Delivery and execution of the CyberStrikeAI agent

Like most C2 agents for Windows, CyberStrikeAI uses PowerShell to execute its payload. When a request is received from the operator, the commands to be executed are additionally encoded in Base64 to bypass keyword-based detection.

Decoded form of the command:

When administrative privileges were available (for example, a domain administrator account), instead of executing commands directly, the agent on remote hosts often created scheduled tasks so that the malicious payload would run with SYSTEM privileges:

An alternative method that does not use schtasks utility is to create a task via the Schedule.Service COM object:

Schedule.Service

The payload (p1.ps1) from the example above is a reverse shell that connects to the server at 185.186.245[.]144:5501:

The p1.ps1 payload and similar scripts were distributed across the network using shared network administrative folders and the WMI protocol, which we will describe in more detail in the Lateral Movement section.

In addition to encoding commands in Base64 and obfuscating SQL/LDAP queries – which we will describe in the Collection & Exfiltration and Discovery sections, respectively – the attackers split the malicious payload into multiple files. It is noteworthy that the scripts were transmitted in this manner even before the agent was installed – that is, at a stage where human intervention is typically required – yet they clearly bear the hallmarks of being generated by an LLM.

Below is a sequential record of several script fragments written to the file d3.b64.

Subsequently, the attackers used the certutil utility to decode the resulting file and executed it with the following command:

Once assembled and decoded, the script’s contents looked like this:

The script is a tool for decrypting DPAPI secrets from the file C:\ProgramData\dsn_line.txt. This file, in turn, is populated by the following command, which searches for a DSN string containing connection settings in the SQL Server Reporting Services configuration file rsreportserver.config and copies its contents to dsn_line.txt.

It is worth noting that some of the scripts delivered and executed as described above contain comments in Chinese (##  –  researcher’s comments).

If the CyberStrikeAI implant was successfully delivered, the first step was to establish persistence on the target system. To do this, the agent created a scheduled task named SystemUpdate , which specified the path to the implant as the action to be performed:

Analysis of the framework’s source code revealed an alternative method of persistence: by adding a value to the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run , where the name of the created value matches the task name ( SystemUpdate ).

HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run

Agent persistence on Linux systems is also implemented in two ways – by adding the entry @reboot <path_to_beacon> & to the user’s crontab (in which case the process runs at system startup), or by adding the line (nohup <path_to_beacon> &>/dev/null &) to ~/.bashrc (in which case the agent starts when an interactive bash shell is opened).

@reboot <path_to_beacon> &

(nohup <path_to_beacon> &>/dev/null &)

It is worth noting that the choice of a specific persistence method is delegated to the LLM connected to CyberStrikeAI. However, thanks to the human-in-the-loop (HITL) mechanism, the operator retains full control over the process: commands generated by the model may require manual approval or correction before they are executed.

Before installing the agent on a compromised host, the attackers manually gathered basic system information using a fairly trivial set of commands:

The attackers also manually checked for internet access and obtained the external IP addresses of the compromised machines using the Chinese service dnslog[.]cn. The service generates a random third-level domain, after which the attackers attempt to resolve it on the compromised machine.

If the machine has internet access, the request succeeds, and the attackers obtain the external IP address of the compromised device on the service’s page.

For reconnaissance purposes, the agent generates a more complex script designed to map out a path for further privilege escalation by compromising SCCM or exploiting msiexec (the AlwaysInstallElevated key):

AlwaysInstallElevated

Additionally, to find ways to elevate privileges locally, the agent executed scripts to inventory services running under domain accounts and tasks running under the SYSTEM account:

During their activity, the attackers periodically checked for Microsoft Defender detections:

After gathering information about the compromised host, the attackers proceeded to conduct reconnaissance within the network. During the preparatory phase of the attack, they manually collected additional information about remote hosts using the net.exe utility.

During the main phase, the agent used PowerShell’s built-in functionality to detect accessible hosts without relying on additional utilities (such as nmap or fscan):

Additionally, relevant LDAP queries to Active Directory objects helped build a network map:

Furthermore, the presence of the installed agent on remote hosts was verified using WMI:

The next step was to gather information about the victims’ domains. To this end, before installing the agent, the attackers used standard OS utilities:

However, later on, using the CyberStrikeAI implant, reconnaissance was carried out via generated PowerShell scripts:

In addition to basic domain information, the agent performed LDAP queries to gather information for Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting attacks:

Finally, the agent was used to check the domain for the presence of LAPS and Microsoft Azure:

To detect signs of Microsoft Azure usage within the infrastructure, the attackers also searched for the .azcopy directory – created by the AzCopy (Microsoft Azure Storage Copy) utility – in users’ home directories:

After successfully conducting reconnaissance and mapping the network, the attackers moved on to the next stage – dumping credentials. For this purpose, the agent used a classic set of LOLBINs and well-known third-party tools.

The agent dumped registry hives containing credentials using the reg.exe utility:

The agent dumped the lsass.exe process using the MiniDump function of the comsvcs.dll library. In doing so, the target process’s PID was used instead of its name to make static detection based on the command line more difficult:

After successfully compromising privileged domain accounts (specifically, the built-in domain administrator), the attackers also carried out DCSync and Golden Ticket attacks via the agent using a renamed version of the mimikatz utility:

To spread across the network using compromised accounts, the attackers employed utilities from the Impacket toolkit, specifically WMIExec, as indicated by the utility’s characteristic command line:

Once installed, the agent prefers to use standard OS mechanisms, such as shared network folders.

Another method the agent uses to remotely execute commands is the WMI protocol. In particular, the agent used it to distribute the aforementioned p1.ps1 reverse shell script. This involved using compromised user accounts with local administrator privileges on the target hosts:

A second method of lateral movement via WMI uses the Invoke-CimMethod cmdlet:

Invoke-CimMethod

To deliver the aforementioned tools (malicious scripts, mimikatz, and the agent itself) to the initial nodes in the infection chain, the attackers used standard OS utilities:

After the agent is installed, it checks the availability of the C2 server’s ports. The implementation mechanisms here are virtually unlimited and depend on the “creativity” of the respective LLM agents connected to the server:

To download additional utilities, the CyberStrikeAI implant also used built-in utilities (LOLBINs). The tools could be hosted on the attackers’ own servers or downloaded directly from GitHub:

The data collection phase deserves special attention. It demonstrates yet another capability of LLM orchestration – the automatic generation of SQL and LDAP queries tailored to a specific task.

In one incident during the campaign, the attackers deployed the CyberStrikeAI impla

articles.title: Filter generation in practice: from algorithms to LLMs
articles.raw_content:
Table of Contents

Filter validity criteria

Problems in filter generation

Filtering security alerts with an algorithm

Pros and cons of the algorithmic approach

Filter generation with an LLM

Pros and cons of generating filters with an LLM

Using multiple AI agents

Pros and cons of the agent-based approach

Evaluating the filter generation system

A modern organization protects its information systems with a whole suite of technologies that generate thousands of security alerts every day. Looking at these alerts in bulk, you’ll see that a significant share are false positives. Ideally, these alerts would be filtered out automatically so that analysts could focus on the ones that may point to a real incident. However, writing filters is a time-consuming task in itself. To create a correct filter, an analyst needs to:

Identify the source of the activity

Define filtering boundaries

Choose filtering criteria

Check that the filter is robust

This post looks at how filter creation itself can be automated to reduce analyst workload.

In the context of security alerts, a filter is a combination of event field values that marks a detection as a false positive and not worth the analyst’s attention. Filters can be generated for any combination of event fields, but not every combination yields a valid filter. That’s why we need to define validity criteria: conditions showing that a specific filter actually removes noise and doesn’t suppress useful alerts.

Detection rules in security systems typically contain a set of conditions, and each of them can generate an alert. A specific event triggers a given fragment of a detection rule. The set of events that a given fragment responds to is what we’ll call its context. A good filter should cover the entire context where possible, without going beyond it. Filters that are too broad or too narrow are useless. For example, a filter based solely on PowerShell would exclude too many events, including some that deserve the analyst’s attention. Most of the filtered events would also be unrelated to the rule in question. A filter on a specific ID, on the other hand, would cover only one event, which may never recur.

We can run into a number of problems when creating filters. First, events often contain an excessive number of fields (around 400 on average), and most of them aren’t needed for filtering. At the same time, generating and ranking combinations of these fields is also fairly resource-intensive. So, the first step is to discard the irrelevant fields and keep only those worth using in the filter. For example, out of 400 fields in an event, four may be enough for filtering.

Another problem is string normalization. Field values (for example, the path to the same application on different systems) can vary depending on system settings, user folder names, and so on. For a filter to account for all these variations, the strings must be normalized. For file paths, in particular, you can replace the drive letter and user folders with standard environment variables and convert all paths to a single case.

Finally, if a filter completely mirrors the query of a detection rule, it effectively disables that rule. To fix this, remove the event fields used in the detection rule from the filter. For example, if a rule triggers on a file path, there are two ways to filter out unwanted alerts:

In the filter, use fields other than the file path.

Use a part of the file path that the rule doesn’t use. For example, for the rule file_path: ".../something.exe" , you can set up a filter that excludes events with the user/unique_files/ directory in the file path.

file_path: ".../something.exe"

user/unique_files/

Given the problems described above, automatically generating filters for security alerts should consist of the following steps:

An analyst receives a security alert that they assess as a false positive and uses the filter generator.

The generator takes the 400-field event from the alert, along with the rule that triggered on it, and determines the context.

The generator selects the fields that are relevant to the filter.

The generator normalizes the strings.

The generator builds different combinations of the selected fields. To do this, we applied the FP-Growth (frequent pattern growth) algorithm to the context determined earlier. FP Growth builds a tree of frequently occurring items (fields) from a dataset (in our case, the context) and discards items that aren’t frequent enough. This reduces the number of combinations to check, which lowers the cost of finding the most relevant ones.

The generator ranks the resulting combinations and offers the analyst the top three to choose from.

For example, consider an event described by the following JSON:

After generating and ranking the combinations, we got three filters based on file paths:

processcmdline:("nodejs\\node.exe" AND "*****\\appdata\\roaming\\npm\/node_modules\/pi-coding-agent\/dist\/cli.js") 1 processcmdline : ( "nodejs\\node.exe" AND "*****\\appdata\\roaming\\npm\/node_modules\/pi-coding-agent\/dist\/cli.js" )

file_path:"*****/.pi\\agent\\bin\\fd.exe" 1 file_path : "*****/.pi\\agent\\bin\\fd.exe"

processcmdline: "programfiles\\nodejs\\node.exe" 1 processcmdline : "programfiles\\nodejs\\node.exe"

The last filter turned out to be too broad, but the analyst marked the other two as valid.

The algorithmic approach to filter generation has several advantages. First, it’s simple and deterministic: the same alert always produces the same result. Second, it’s interpretable, meaning we can see why a given combination ranked near the top of the list and why a particular field didn’t make it into the list of candidate fields at all. Third, the stages of the process are independent of each other, so individual steps can be improved and tuned without the risk of breaking the algorithm elsewhere. Finally, it has no external dependencies or models, which makes it easy to deploy in any customer environment.

However, it also has drawbacks. The first is its dependence on context. If there’s no context for some reason — for example, the rule’s first-ever trigger — a filter can’t be created. The second problem is string normalization. There’s a high chance of running into atypical cases that the normalization rules don’t cover. Often such cases can’t be described correctly at all, because they contradict each other.

These problems can be solved with large language models (LLMs). When an LLM generates the filters, no context is needed, because the LLM doesn’t iterate over or rank combinations. The LLM also takes a more flexible approach to string normalization, including non-standard cases. That said, an LLM doesn’t have to be involved at every stage of the generation process. We decided to keep the algorithmic solution where it works well. For example, a simple algorithm selects suitable fields without errors, so we didn’t move this stage to the model.

The LLM-based filter generation looks like this:

The input is still an alert containing an event with 400 fields, plus the rule that triggered on that event. Then an algorithm selects the most suitable fields for the filter. Next, the LLM processes the input — the event, the selected fields, and the detection rule — and generates three filter options along with an explanation for them. The explanation helps the analyst understand why these particular filters were suggested and make an informed choice.

Consider the following event in JSON format:

The LLM suggested three filter options that all contain the same command line fragment:

file_path: "\\WindowsPowerShell\\powershell.exe" AND filecmdline: "Get-VM -Name kafka\*" 1 file_path : "\\WindowsPowerShell\\powershell.exe" AND filecmdline : "Get-VM -Name kafka\*"

filecmdline: "Get-VM -Name kafka\*" 1 filecmdline : "Get-VM -Name kafka\*"

filecmdline: "kafka*" 1 filecmdline : "kafka*"

As in the previous example, two of the three output filters were valid. The last one was too broad to be usable. The analyst chose the first filter with minor edits:

Using an LLM solved the problems of purely algorithmic filter generation: dependence on context and errors in string normalization. However, the single-request approach had its own drawbacks. First, it had no output validation. The LLM returned filters as-is, with no syntax check and no way to correct errors. Second, unlike in the algorithmic version, all filter generation tasks were handled by a single system prompt. As a result, a minor fix in one place could break the logic in another.

To address the problems of generating filters with a single model and a single system prompt, we tried distributing the tasks across different LLM agents. In this version, we brought in agents as early as the stage of selecting relevant fields. The chain includes four agents in total:

Selector: selects the relevant fields.

Generator: generates filters.

Validator: evaluates the generated filters. If the filters are found to be invalid, it returns the task to the generator. If the selected fields are found to be irrelevant, it starts a new field selection cycle. If the filters pass validation, or the limit on regeneration attempts is reached, the valid filters (or the best ones available) are passed to the analyst.

Commentator: analyzes the output filters and explains which field values were used and why.

For the following JSON event, the agents produce three valid filters based on the file path.

The filters differ in the additional parameters that support the detection:

file_path:"sysvol\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat" 1 file_path : "sysvol\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat"

file_path:"sysvol\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat" AND file_md5:"0x7..6E" 1 file_path : "sysvol\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat" AND file_md5 : "0x7..6E"

autorun_entry: "Group Policy\\State" AND file_path: "SYSVOL\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat" 1 autorun_entry : "Group Policy\\State" AND file_path : "SYSVOL\\domain\\scripts\\logon.bat"

LLM agents give us a system that can validate and correct filters. Its modular architecture also lets us tune and improve different stages of generation independently. However, this approach makes more LLM calls than the previous ones, so the system is slower. It also depends on access to a model, which may not be available in the organization’s isolated environment.

To evaluate how well the filter generation system works, we use two main metrics:

Approval rate. For each security alert, the system suggests three filters. If the analyst selects at least one of them, we count the generation as successful. For example, in the case below, the approval rate is 2/3.

False positive reduction rate (FP drop). This metric shows how much a filter helps reduce the number of false positives. It can only be measured over time, because we need to compare the number of false positive alerts received during a set period before and after the filter is deployed.

Below is a comparison of the three filter generation approaches by these metrics:

As the results show, LLMs significantly improve the efficiency of filter generation. At the same time, the LLM agentless and agent-based approaches perform almost identically. So we chose the simpler and faster option: an LLM with a single system prompt. As a result, we cut false positives by 99%, increased the number of filters generated per day by 28%, and made analysts’ alert handling 17% more efficient.

Practice has shown that filter generation can be automated effectively. We’ve looked at several options for automatically generating filters for false-positive security alerts: a purely algorithmic approach, an LLM-based approach, and an approach built on a group of LLM agents. All of them can generate valid filters and make the analyst’s work much easier, but each has its own pros and cons.

The algorithmic approach scored lower on the evaluation metrics, but in two-thirds of cases, it still produces filters that satisfy the analyst. It works especially well when there’s already a set of similar events to filter out, meaning enough context has accumulated. The algorithmic generator can also be deployed in any environment. Both standalone LLM and multi-agent LLM approaches show high accuracy, and their results differ only slightly, so the slower agent-based approach looks excessive at this stage. If an LLM is available, the best option appears to be a single model that handles several stages of the generation cycle.

Machine learning

Artificial intelligence

This is an interesting topic with huge potential to expand. A SOC is a service that operates almost entirely on text data, making it one of the prime candidates whose workload can and SHOULD be fully delegated to AI agents. It just depends on how the org sets up this process. Generating filters for SOC rules is just one aspect of a potentially autonomous workflow where human intervention drops to zero. Using a standart LLM pipeline to write filters makes an analyst’s life easier, but using full agent orchestration for a simple task that will just be manually verified by an analyst anyway doesn’t make much sense. In a true agentic setup, a human should only intervene when there’s strong evidence of smth highly unusual happening in the system. The rest of the time, the harness should build graphs of logical decision, calculate further steps, and use underlying models for reasoning. Easy to say, hard to implement of course.. The cost of deploying and maintaining such a system can be very high. Not to mention that alongside frontier AI models, a closed agentic loop needs a solid harness, custom tools, MCP servers, skills, etc. And all these components must work seamlessly. Reply

articles.title: Unknown APT uses NetamLoader to attack a Win10 OS customized for governments in Asia
articles.raw_content:
Table of Contents

Initial infection

AES encryption scheme for network traffic

Discovering proxies

Execute downloaded XAML payload in an isolated AppDomain

Indicators of Compromise

A couple of months ago, our research revealed a highly sophisticated infection chain and a complex .NET assembly-loading framework built on XAML markup, which strongly indicates a supply-chain attack targeting a custom Windows build used exclusively by government entities in Asia. The malicious framework has been labeled NetamLoader; at present, no attribution to any known APT group has been established.

The sample came to light in the first half of 2026, when Kaspersky Security Network (KSN) issued a malware detection alert for a .config file using AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. The file was packaged inside a CAB archive placed in the directory that stores Windows operating system update packages. Initial analysis of the CAB contents found no malicious code: most executables were legitimate components of the third-party patch management tool Patch My PC, and even the .NET assemblies used for the injection were Microsoft-signed. A later re-examination of the original .config file and the full loading process revealed the infection chain and framework described in this report.

Kaspersky’s products detect this threat as HEUR:Trojan.MSIL.NetamLoader.gen, Trojan.MSIL.Zapchast.*, and Trojan.Script.Agent.*.

During routine threat hunting, KSN sent us a malware detection alert. The notification flagged a .config file that employed AppDomainManager injection to load arbitrary .NET assemblies. The file was compressed into a CAB archive named e4537a1762fcafd2fd96bfc825bad34f9db9a24d and saved in the folder that stores Windows operating system update packages. Below is the full path to this archive:

Starting with this CAB archive, we uncovered a highly complex infection chain that uses a previously unknown advanced loading framework.

The CAB file contains the following seven files, which are extracted and placed in the path C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\Download\Install\:

Files compressed in the CAB file Except for Resources.resx, none of the files contain malicious code. We did not observe how the CAB file was delivered to the victim; we only saw the process PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe running with the following arguments:

Files compressed in the CAB file

After the file is launched in this manner, the infection chain progresses to stage 1.

Starting with the execution of PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe, which then served as a host process for loading several payloads, we identified a complex two‑stage loading mechanism with multiple steps. The overall flow of stage 1 is summarized in the diagram below.

Infection chain: Stage 1

The AppDomainManager injection technique is used to load an arbitrary .NET assembly. With this mechanism, when PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe runs, the accompanying configuration file PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config in the same directory is loaded before the executable’s main function runs. Below is the content of PatchMyPC‑ScriptRunner.exe.config.

According to the configuration file, the class Microsoft.ApplicationServer.Caching.DataCacheFactoryConfiguration from the Microsoft.HostIntegration.Connectors.dll module (a Microsoft‑signed assembly) is loaded. DataCacheFactoryConfiguration is the configuration class for the Windows Server AppFabric Cache Client, specifying the settings for a new cache client. When the configuration class is loaded, its instance first attempts to find and read the default configuration file, fabric.config, located in the same directory. The contents of fabric.config are shown below:

Microsoft.ApplicationServer.Caching.DataCacheFactoryConfiguration

DataCacheFactoryConfiguration

The DataCacheFactoryConfiguration class has a design flaw that can be abused to load arbitrary assemblies. The fabric.config file is meticulously crafted. When the file is loaded, the DataCacheFactoryConfiguration instance examines its className attribute, loads the specified type ( System.Resources.ResXResourceSet from the System.Windows.Forms assembly), and creates a ResXResourceSet instance, passing “Resources.resx” to its constructor for parsing.

DataCacheFactoryConfiguration

DataCacheFactoryConfiguration

System.Resources.ResXResourceSet

System.Windows.Forms

In the .resx file, multiple layers of payloads – including several XAML files, .NET assemblies, and JSON data – are encoded, compressed, or encrypted (see the diagram below). Each layer is unpacked and loaded by the layer above it. Once a layer finishes its operation, the next layer is extracted and loaded. Below, we analyze each layer in the order in which it is loaded:

Multiple layers of payloads are compressed and encrypted in the .resx file

The Microsoft RESX schema defines the XML layout used by .resx files, which has a human-readable structure and can hold application resources: strings, images, icons, and serialized objects. The Resources.resx file contains a Base64‑encoded binary object that was serialized using the well‑known, highly vulnerable .NET BinaryFormatter class.

Base64-encoded serialized binary object in Resources.resx

Parsing this .resx file with ResXResourceSet causes the embedded Base64‑encoded binary payload to invoke BinaryFormatter.Deserialize(), triggering a deserialization vulnerability that enables a TypeConfuseDelegate attack . The TypeConfuseDelegate then invokes XamlReader.Parse() , which loads a XAML payload (named XAML-1) embedded within the binary object.

XamlReader.Parse()

XAML is a markup language for building user interfaces in .NET applications, but its capabilities extend far beyond that. Using two built‑in objects, ObjectDataProvider and ResourceDictionary , logic equivalent to C# code can be expressed in an XML‑like syntax. A code snippet of XAML-1

A code snippet of XAML-1

The XAML-1 code acts as a loader for an embedded payload. The process is as follows:

Retrieve the full command line of the current host process PatchMyPC‑ScriptRunner.exe, converting all arguments to lowercase.

Generate the AES key by hashing the command‑line string with SHA‑256.

Decode the Base64 string embedded in XAML-1 into a binary array. Use the first 16 bytes of that array as the IV, then decrypt the remaining encrypted data with AES. The decrypted output is another piece of XAML code, which we refer to as XAML-2.

Load XAML-2 into memory using the .NET API System.Windows.Markup.XamlReader.Load() .

If any exception occurs during decryption, trigger Environment.Exit(0) , silently terminating the host process to prevent error messages that might reveal the attack.

Environment.Exit(0)

XAML‑2 initiates stage 2 of the infection. The diagram below shows the overall flow of this stage. Infection chain: Stage 2

Infection chain: Stage 2

XAML‑2 contains two embedded Base64‑encoded sections. These sections are actually two additional XAML files (referred to as XAML-2-1 and XAML-2-2) that were first compressed with ZIP and then encoded in Base64. After decoding and decompressing, XAML-2 loads each file into memory separately with XamlReader.Load() . A code snippet of XAML-2

XamlReader.Load()

A code snippet of XAML-2

The first file consists of 796 lines. Its sole purpose is to hijack a key AMSI API to bypass anti‑malware scanning.

Sensitive strings in XAML-2-1 are cut into tiny pieces

To avoid detection by anti‑malware signature scans, sensitive strings are split into very short fragments. When XAML-2-1 is loaded and parsed, the fragments are reassembled into the original string.

The key steps it takes to achieve its goal are as follows:

Check the OS architecture by verifying whether IntPtr.Size equals 8. If it does not, the host process isn’t 64‑bit, so abort the hijack operation.

Combine the split strings into a single CLSID GUID (fdb00e52-a214-4aa1-8fba-4357bb0072ec), then try to create an instance of the AMSI COM object using this GUID.

Patch the AMSI module. Create a delegate for the runtime method Console.Clear() and then obtain its native function pointer. Next, patch the method by overwriting its first bytes in memory with the binary payload (41 C7 00 01 00 00 00 33 C0 C3). Obtain the native pointer of the AMSI COM object with Marshal.GetIUnknownForObject() . From this pointer, read the address of its virtual method table and add 0x18 to reach another pointer that holds the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan method. Use VirtualProtect() to make the Scan() pointer writable, change its value from the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan() method to the address of the patched Console.Clear() , and then restore the pointer’s original protection attributes. Once this step is complete, every scan returns AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (value = 0) .

Create a delegate for the runtime method Console.Clear() and then obtain its native function pointer. Next, patch the method by overwriting its first bytes in memory with the binary payload (41 C7 00 01 00 00 00 33 C0 C3).

Obtain the native pointer of the AMSI COM object with Marshal.GetIUnknownForObject() . From this pointer, read the address of its virtual method table and add 0x18 to reach another pointer that holds the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan method.

Marshal.GetIUnknownForObject()

CAmsiAntimalware::Scan

Use VirtualProtect() to make the Scan() pointer writable, change its value from the address of the CAmsiAntimalware::Scan() method to the address of the patched Console.Clear() , and then restore the pointer’s original protection attributes. Once this step is complete, every scan returns AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (value = 0) .

VirtualProtect()

CAmsiAntimalware::Scan()

AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN (value = 0)

One patch targets the Console.Clear() API, which resides in the memory space of an existing legitimate module, while the other modifies only the virtual tables of the AMSI module, allowing the malware to pass code integrity checks.

XAML-2-2 consists of two parts: a .NET module (the first loader, .NET 1 Loader) and a JSON data payload (the C2 configuration, JSON-1). Both components are compressed with ZIP and then encoded in Base64. XAML-2-2 first decodes and decompresses the .NET assembly .NET 1 Loader, then uses the Assembly.CreateInstance() API to create an instance of the .NET 1 Loader and passes the Base64‑encoded JSON-1 to the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader as a parameter.

Assembly.CreateInstance()

.NET 1 Loader decodes, decompresses, and parses JSON‑1. The decoded and decompressed JSON‑1 is shown below:

JSON-1-c This JSON contains the configuration data that .NET 1 Loader uses to report the execution results of the loaded payload to the C2 server. sc false Flag. Determines whether to report the execution result of m.C() . When set to false, reporting to C2 is skipped. c null Reporting C2 server. The result returned by the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader is sent to this server. tp null Unknown item, suspected to be a trusted SSL certificate. Thumbprint was used to verify this alleged C2 certificate. e null The AES key that encrypts the JSON result returned by the m.C() method of .NET 1 Loader.

JSON-1-p JSON-1-p is a more complex configuration file. .NET 1 Loader parses its data to prepare and load the subsequent stages. The following configuration keys store the payloads: oib : Base64‑encoded .NET 2 Plugin (PE file) oub : Base64‑encoded XAML that invokes Exit(0) ibk : AES key used to decrypt ibi ibi : A Base64‑encoded collection of compressed, encrypted XAML templates used to build XAML-3. Detailed instructions for decrypting and assembling XAML‑3 are provided in the XAML‑3 section below. Other items are passed as C2 configuration to the .NET 2 Plugin at a later stage. [

After obtaining the configuration, .NET 1 Loader proceeds with the following key steps:

Delete the update records from the system log related to the malicious update packages, along with the malicious files and cache files used in stage 1. Delete malicious files extracted from the CAB PatchMyPC-ScriptRunner.exe.config

Read the files’ contents, filter out any lines containing the exact substring GetExtendedUpdateInfoHandler, and write the filtered content back to the log files. The path contains the keyword CmitUpdateAgent, which may be linked to a custom Windows 10 build used by a government in Asia. "%WINDIR%\Logs\CmitUpdateAgent\20????\20??????" 1 "%WINDIR%\Logs\CmitUpdateAgent\20????\20??????" Of the nine GUIDs derived using this method, one indicates that an exception occurred, and the others are numbered 0 through 7. For example, when the malware catches exception code 129, it creates the registry subkey {bde7ddc2-1f6f-4397-a0df-ae7c7d67d65a} to indicate that an exception occurred. articles.title: Millions of security cameras at risk: DoS vulnerability in Intelbras devices
articles.raw_content:
Table of Contents

How authentication works

Affected endpoint

PoC: vulnerability exploitation

New firmware version

Network-connected surveillance cameras are now widespread in both home and enterprise environments, so securing them is essential to safeguarding physical spaces and sensitive assets. As these devices continue to gain new features and network connectivity capabilities, vulnerabilities in their implementation can have significant security implications.

During our research, we discovered a denial-of-service vulnerability that affects Intelbras IP cameras systems. The flaw resides in a firmware update endpoint that is accessible without authentication and allows anyone with access to the local Wi-Fi network to knock cameras offline. A single request disrupts the camera for only about a minute, but sending periodic requests keeps the device offline indefinitely. We reported the issue to Intelbras, monitored the remediation process, validated the fix in the new firmware, and will now demonstrate the exploitation procedure step-by-step.

Following our notification, Intelbras patched the vulnerability and released updated firmware ( R.260804 ) along with update instructions . A candidate ID of CAN-2026-2035970 has been assigned by MITRE following submission, pending the final CVE assignment. Additionally, the Intelbras team recently informed us that MITRE has classified the vulnerability as Medium, assigning it a score of 5.1 under the CVSS 4.0 framework. The issue discussed in this article is no longer present in the latest firmware version.

Intelbras provides firmware files on its official website. While users can manually install these updates via an SD card, the cameras also natively support firmware upgrades over the local network via their web interface and mobile app. We obtained the firmware version v240927 for the iM3B-C (IM3 C) camera, which was the latest available version at the time of our research. According to Intelbras, the same firmware is also compatible with the iMX C, iM4 C, iM5 SC, iME 360 C, and iM7+ FC models. Below, we can view the firmware version and the camera model used as an example.

To provide context, we will explain how the camera’s authentication mechanism works and why it is relevant to accessing the camera’s endpoints. The main firmware component is an ARM binary named sonia , responsible for controlling the kernel drivers used by the camera hardware, authentication, and livestream recording, among other things.

The global.login RPC method handles authentication at the /RPC2_Login endpoint. First, the client, such as the mobile app or a custom script, sends the username and an empty password. The camera responds with an authentication challenge (a set of values to verify the password without transmitting it). This response returns a temporary session, the encryption type in the encryption field, a random value, and a realm (authentication scope). At this stage, a false response is normal and does not indicate a failed login, as the authentication process is not yet complete.

Next, the client calculates the response password from the authentication challenge . It first generates an MD5 (username:realm:original_password) hash as the base. It then calculates a second MD5 (username:random:first_md5) hash,  where first_md5 is the result of the previous step . To complete the authentication, the client sends this final result back to /RPC2_Login in a second global.login call, passing the username, calculated password, and temporary session ID.

If the login is accepted, the camera returns true and a new, authenticated session. This session must be used for all subsequent RPC calls, including the camera’s other endpoints, for example, the one that reboots the device or those that expose sensitive information.

The affected endpoint is the firmware upgrade route http://<ip_address>/firmwareUpgrade_service/Demo , which lacks authentication checks; furthermore, it fails to verify whether the firmware is actually valid before initiating the upgrade process. This creates a serious issue because the upgrade requires the camera to reboot, and that is precisely when the problem occurs: the camera enters reboot mode and eventually shuts down, appearing offline to the user and anyone who has the camera registered on their device.

Now that we have outlined how the vulnerability works, we will use a Python script on an iM3B-C camera to exploit it for demonstration purposes. The exploit contacts the camera’s endpoint to upload firmware. Below, we can see sonia creating the endpoint responsible for the firmware upgrade.

Next, the exploit will hit the endpoint and cause the camera to reboot. Consequently, mobile phones running the Intelbras app will lose connection with the registered device. Below, we can see the camera operating normally: the green light is on and the app is showing it is available for viewing.

The camera is online

After the exploit executes, we can see the effects: the camera goes offline and loses connection to the registered devices.

The camera is offline

The exploit is quite simple: it sends an HTTP POST request with the firmware, which causes the camera to accept the request and initiate the reboot process. It does not matter whether the firmware is original; the reboot process will start regardless.

After we notified Intelbras about this flaw in the endpoint implementation, the company contacted the OEM vendor. As a result, a new firmware version was released that requires authentication to initiate an update through this endpoint.

Below, we can compare the new firmware, which validates cookies and session data, with the old firmware, which performed no authentication checks and proceeded directly to the update routine.

An attacker can remotely trigger the camera firmware upgrade and reboot process without authenticating or supplying a valid firmware image. This may cause the device to go offline, which results in a denial-of-service condition preventing legitimate users from accessing live monitoring or managing the camera.

The potential impact is significant due to the number of affected users. The Intelbras Mibo Smart app , which the company provides to connect and manage the devices mentioned in this report, has over 4,000,000 downloads. Brazil represents the largest user base, followed by Paraguay, Ecuador, Colombia, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Uruguay, and Venezuela. As a result, exploitation of this issue affects a large number of users.

This is a medium-severity vulnerability that Intelbras is already aware of. The issue has been addressed in a newer firmware release ( R.260804 along with update instructions ), which mitigates this attack vector. Because the vulnerability directly affects the availability and normal operation of the affected cameras, it is highly recommended that users verify the firmware version currently installed on their devices and update to the latest available version as soon as possible. Keeping the firmware up to date is an essential security practice, especially for internet-connected surveillance devices, as outdated versions may remain exposed to known vulnerabilities.

By: Matt Brady Jared Valentine

Categories: Hospitality Hacks and Retail Reality Checks Insights

Hospitality Hacks and Retail Reality Checks

Unit 42 has been actively monitoring for new developments related to the cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems in Europe since at least October 2026. The unidentified threat actors gained unauthorized access to refrigeration controllers and set them to defrost mode, resulting in hundreds of supermarkets across the region having to throw away spoiled food. The time of year when this activity has occurred is particularly concerning since retailers need to maintain adequate inventory levels as shoppers ramp up spending during holiday periods.

Here we provide a high-level overview of the attacks based on public reporting and explore insights on device exposure by country, based on our findings using Cortex Xpanse . It also explores how Palo Alto Networks customers can leverage existing products and Unit 42 services to reduce their attack surface to mitigate similar threat activity in the future.

The first wave of these attacks occurred overnight between Oct. 11–12, 2026, primarily targeting approximately 700 supermarkets in France. Since that time, another wave occurred overnight between Nov. 1–2, 2026, expanding across at least 10 additional European countries and impacting over 100–115 retail locations.

In addition to the aforementioned activity, French authorities recently disclosed that refrigeration systems used by medical facilities were impacted by the attacks. At this time, there’s no evidence to suggest blood products were spoiled as a result.

According to multiple sources, the threat actors behind the supermarket activities raised the temperature of the targeted refrigeration units as high as 50°C (122°F). In some cases, the activity resulted in fires. The initial access vector currently remains unconfirmed. However, there is widespread speculation that impacted devices were potentially running vulnerable versions of software and/or used default credentials provided by the manufacturers that attackers easily identified.

From Nov. 5–6, 2026, we identified the presence of over 5,000 devices exposed to the internet that were manufactured by companies listed in the CERT-FR advisory last month. These statistics do not necessarily mean that the devices are running vulnerable versions of software that could’ve been exploited. High Profile Threats

Published: October 29, 2026

Categories: High Profile Threats Vulnerabilities

High Profile Threats

Tags: CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619 PHP2Shell

Unit 42 is aware of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, referred to as PHP2Shell. Both are remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities rated as 9.2 (CVSS 4.0). We encourage reviewing the PHP Group’s security advisory and patching guidance .

PHP is widely used across web servers and content management systems globally. We recommend assessing your exposure to these vulnerabilities and patching immediately.

Palo Alto Networks has evaluated our product portfolio regarding this issue. Refer to our security advisory for the most up to date details.

CVE-2026-109618 involves a remote code execution vulnerability where handling out-of-memory errors via longjmp() leaves request memory uninitialized due to improper control flow management, allowing attackers to reliably achieve RCE using out-of-memory (OOM) triggers.

CVE-2026-109619 describes a remote code execution vulnerability where longjmp() fatal error handling leaves global memory pointing to freed memory regions. These regions can later be read or branched on during subsequent requests, enabling attackers to execute arbitrary code.

At the time of publication, Palo Alto Networks Cortex Xpanse has identified the presence of over 22.6 million exposed instances potentially vulnerable to CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 based on our telemetry.

As disclosed in our security advisory , the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are being actively exploited against PAN-OS management interfaces that are exposed to the internet. Dream Research has reported a campaign in which attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation vulnerability to gain root access. Unit 42 has independently verified the same attacker’s tooling and confirmed the reported results.

By default the management interface is not exposed to the internet per security best practices ; customers should immediately remove public internet access to management interfaces if it is enabled. Customers should also restrict management access to trusted internal IP addresses, and apply available PAN-OS fixes addressing PHP2Shell. Customers who have applied the available patches are not affected. These fixes interrupt the observed exploit chain. Our security advisory provides affected versions, patch availability and mitigation requirements. The Workarounds and Mitigations section of our security advisory also provides details of how Advanced Threat Prevention signatures provide coverage against this vulnerability.

Only a small fraction of a percent (approximately .02%) of our global installed base has internet-facing management interfaces configured and were impacted. Each of these customers has been individually contacted by our teams. We will continue to investigate and provide any necessary updates as they become available.
